lessons.title: Vectors
lessons.book_section: 8.1 Storing Lists of Values with Vectors → Creating a New Vector, Updating a Vector, Reading Elements of Vectors
lessons.objective_md: Create and grow a `Vec<T>`, read its elements with indexing or `get` and say which one panics, and explain why holding a reference to an element blocks `push` (E0502).

screens.heading: A list that can grow
screens.text_md:
An array has a fixed length: `fixed` holds 3 numbers for as long as it exists. A **vector**, written `Vec<T>`, can grow and shrink while the program runs, because it keeps its elements in a buffer on the heap.

`T` is the element type. `growable` is a `Vec<i32>`: every element is an `i32`, so the elements sit next to each other in memory. `push` changes the vector, so it must be `mut`. This program prints `3 4`.

coming_from.c: `Vec<T>` is Rust's `std::vector<T>`: a pointer, a length and a capacity, with the elements in one heap buffer. Like a `std::vector`, it frees that buffer when it goes out of scope.
coming_from.go: `Vec<T>` is like a Go slice used with `append`. In Rust, `push` changes the vector in place; you don't assign a result back.
coming_from.java: `Vec<T>` plays the role of Java's `ArrayList<T>` or C#'s `List<T>`. It stores `i32` values directly, with no boxing into `Integer` objects.
coming_from.js: A `Vec<T>` is like a TypeScript `T[]`: it grows with `push`. Unlike JavaScript, every element must have the same type, and the compiler checks it.
coming_from.python: A `Vec` is like a Python `list`, with one difference: every element has the same type. A `Vec<i32>` can't also hold a string.

screens.heading: Three ways to make a vector
screens.text_md:
`Vec::new()` makes an empty vector. Nothing inside tells Rust what it will hold, so you write the type: `Vec<i32>`. If you `push` an `i32` later, Rust can infer the type from that instead.

The `vec!` macro builds a vector from values, and Rust infers `Vec<i32>` from them. `vec![0; 3]` repeats one value: three zeros. `{:?}` prints a whole vector: `[] [2, 3, 5, 7] [0, 0, 0]`.

steps.caption_md: `vec!` puts the three elements in one heap buffer with room for exactly three. `v` itself only holds a pointer to the buffer, the **length** (elements in use) and the **capacity** (room available).
steps.visual_md: Stack box `v` (ptr ●, len 3, cap 3); arrow to heap buffer A with cells 1 2 3, all filled

steps.caption_md: Buffer A is full, so `push` asks for a bigger buffer, which may be somewhere else in memory. The elements are moved into it and the old buffer is freed. This is why a vector can grow without limit.
steps.visual_md: Heap buffer A greyed out, labelled "freed"; new heap buffer B with cells 1 2 3 4 and spare empty cells; `v` now shows len 4, cap ≥ 4, arrow to B

steps.caption_md: A vector grows by more than one slot at a time, so this `push` usually finds spare room and writes 5 straight into the same buffer.
steps.visual_md: Buffer B with cells 1 2 3 4 5; `v` shows len 5, arrow still to B

steps.caption_md: `len()` counts the elements, not the capacity. When `v` goes out of scope at the end of `main`, the buffer and every element in it are freed.
steps.visual_md: Same as step 3; output panel: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] has 5 elements

question.prompt_md: Which line creates a vector holding the four values `7, 7, 7, 7`?

explanations.text_md: Correct. `vec![value; count]` repeats the value: four sevens in a `Vec<i32>` that can still grow.
Not quite. The value comes first and the count second, so this makes seven fours: `[4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4]`.
Not quite. Without `vec!` this is an array of four sevens. Its length is fixed at 4, so it has no `push`.
Not quite. `Vec::new` takes no arguments and always makes an empty vector; this line is a compile error (E0061).

screens.heading: Reading an element: `v[i]` or `v.get(i)`
screens.text_md:
Positions start at 0, so index 2 is the third element. `&v[2]` gives a reference to it, without copying it out of the vector.

`v.get(2)` finds the same element but returns an `Option<&i32>`: `Some(&30)` when the index is in range, `None` when it isn't. Both print 30 here. The difference shows up when the index is too big, as the next two screens show.

screens.heading: `v[100]` stops the program
screens.text_md:
This compiles: the compiler doesn't track how many elements a vector will hold. When the line runs, `v[100]` checks the index, finds it past the end and **panics**: the program stops with a message instead of reading memory that isn't part of the vector.

Use `v[i]` when an index out of range would be a bug you want to hear about loudly.

coming_from.c: Unlike `std::vector`'s `operator[]`, Rust's `v[i]` is always bounds-checked, so it can't read past the end. It behaves like `at()`, except it panics instead of throwing.
coming_from.go: Same as Go: indexing past the end of a slice panics with "index out of range". Rust adds `get`, which returns `None` instead of panicking.
coming_from.java: Like `list.get(100)` throwing `IndexOutOfBoundsException` (or `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` in C#), but a panic isn't caught with `try`. Use `get` when a missing element is a normal case.
coming_from.js: `arr[100]` in JavaScript quietly gives `undefined`. Rust's `v[100]` stops the program instead; `v.get(100)` is the version that hands back "nothing" (`None`) for you to handle.
coming_from.python: Like `lst[100]` raising `IndexError`, except a Rust panic isn't something you catch: the program stops. For "maybe there's an element", use `get`, which returns an `Option`.

screens.heading: `get` lets you plan for a missing element
screens.text_md:
`get` checks the index too, but instead of panicking it returns `None`, and `match` makes you decide what that means. Here the program prints `there is no element 100` and carries on.

Use `get` when an index out of range is a normal event, for example a position a user typed. Use `v[i]` when you know the index is valid.

screens.heading: A reference into the vector blocks `push`
screens.text_md:
This looks harmless: you read the first element, then add one at the end. But it breaks the borrowing rule from Chapter 4: while a shared reference into `v` is still in use, nothing may borrow `v` mutably. `first` is used on line 5, so its borrow covers line 4.

The next screen shows why the rule matters for vectors in particular.

annotations.note_md: line 3: `first` is a shared reference to an element inside `v`.
line 4: `push` needs `&mut v`, exclusive access to the whole vector.
line 5: `first` is still needed after the push, so its borrow overlaps the mutable one.

screens.heading: Why: `push` might move the element away
screens.text_md:
Elements of a vector sit next to each other in one buffer. If the buffer is full, `push` allocates a bigger one, moves the elements there and frees the old one. `first` would then point at freed memory.

The compiler doesn't know whether a particular `push` will need to grow, so it rejects every `push` while a reference into the vector is still in use. That rule is what makes the dangling arrow on the right impossible in safe Rust.

coming_from.c: This is iterator and pointer invalidation: `push_back` on a full `std::vector` invalidates every pointer into it. In C++ that's undefined behaviour you must avoid by hand; Rust refuses to compile it.
coming_from.go: Go's `append` can also copy the slice to a new array, leaving an old pointer to stale data. Go keeps the old array alive; Rust frees it, so it forbids the stale pointer instead.
coming_from.java: Close to Java's `ConcurrentModificationException`, but caught at compile time and for a deeper reason: the element itself could move, not just an iterator's bookkeeping.
coming_from.js: JavaScript arrays reallocate behind the scenes too, but you can't hold a reference to an array slot. Rust lets you borrow a slot directly, and the borrow checker makes sure the slot can't move while you hold it.
coming_from.python: Python lists also move their storage when they grow, but Python never gives you a pointer into that storage, only to the objects. Rust references point at the elements themselves, so the compiler has to guard them.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `v[0]` without `&` copies the `i32` out of the vector, because `i32` is `Copy`. `first` holds its own number, not a reference into the buffer, so the push is allowed. It prints `first is 1`.
Not quite. E0502 needs a reference into the vector (`&v[0]`) that is still in use. Here the number was copied, so nothing points into the buffer when `push` runs.

screens.heading: End the borrow, then push
screens.text_md:
A borrow lasts until the reference's last use, not until the end of the block. `first` is last used on line 4, so by the time `push` runs on line 5, nothing points into `v` and the mutable borrow is allowed.

So the fix is to finish with the reference before you change the vector, or to copy a `Copy` element out with `let first = v[0];` as in the quick check.

question.prompt_md: Which change makes the program from screen 7 compile, while it still prints the first element through `first`?

options.text_md: Create the vector with `Vec::with_capacity(10)` so `push` never needs a new buffer

explanations.text_md: Correct. `first` is then last used before `push`, so its shared borrow has ended when the mutable borrow starts.
Not quite. A mutable reference to an element is still a borrow of `v`, and `push` can't take a second mutable borrow while it's in use: error E0499.
Not quite. The borrow checker never looks at capacity. It rejects any `push` while a reference into the vector is still in use, so this is still E0502.
Not quite. `mut` on `first` only lets you point `first` at something else. It doesn't end the borrow of `v`, so this is still E0502 (plus an unused-`mut` warning).

summary: A `Vec<T>` holds any number of values of one type `T` in one heap buffer. Make one with `Vec::new()` (writing the type if Rust can't infer it), `vec![a, b, c]` or `vec![value; count]`.
`push` adds to the end and needs a `mut` vector. When the buffer is full, the vector moves its elements to a bigger buffer.
`&v[i]` panics at run time if `i` is out of range; `v.get(i)` returns `Option<&T>`, with `None` for a missing element.
Holding a reference into a vector while calling `push` is error E0502, because the push could move the element the reference points at.
Finish using the reference before you push, or copy a `Copy` element out with `v[i]`.

lessons.title: Iterating vectors, and vectors of enums
lessons.book_section: 8.1 Storing Lists of Values with Vectors → Iterating Over the Values in a Vector, Using an Enum to Store Multiple Types (plus common vector methods, course addition)
lessons.objective_md: Loop over a vector to read (`&v`), change (`&mut v` with `*`) or consume (`v`) its elements, store different kinds of values in one vector with an enum, and use the common vector methods.

screens.heading: Reading every element with `for x in &v`

steps.caption_md: Before the loop, `total` starts at 0. Looping over a vector is safer than counting indexes yourself: there's no index that can run past the end.
`for x in &v` borrows the vector and hands you a **reference** to each element in turn, so `x` is a `&i32`. `*x` follows the reference to the number it points at.
steps.visual_md: Rows: `v` = `[100, 32, 57]` with cell 100 outlined blue ("borrowed"), `x` = `&100`, `total` = `100`; `x` and `total` highlighted

steps.caption_md: Second element: `total` is now 132. Nothing was copied out of the vector; `x` only points at each element.
steps.visual_md: Rows: `v` with cell 32 outlined blue, `x` = `&32`, `total` = `132`; `x` and `total` highlighted

steps.caption_md: Third and last element: `total` is 189. After the last element the loop ends, and so does its borrow of `v`.
steps.visual_md: Rows: `v` with cell 57 outlined blue, `x` = `&57`, `total` = `189`; `x` and `total` highlighted

steps.caption_md: The loop only borrowed `v`, so `v.len()` still works after it: `189 from 3 items`.
steps.visual_md: Rows: `v` = `[100, 32, 57]`, `total` = `189`; row `x` struck through (out of scope); output panel: 189 from 3 items

screens.heading: Changing every element with `for x in &mut v`
screens.text_md:
`for x in &mut v` hands out a **mutable reference** to each element, so the loop can change the elements in place. The vector itself must be `mut`.

`x` is a `&mut i32`, a pointer to the element, so you write `*x` to reach the number. `*x += 50` adds 50 to the element; plain `x += 50` would try to add to the reference itself, and the compiler rejects that (E0368). This program prints `[150, 82, 107]`.

screens.heading: `for x in v` uses the vector up

left.label: Doesn't compile
left.caption_md: `for x in v` moves the vector into the loop, which hands out the elements themselves. Line 6 then fails with E0382, borrow of moved value: `v`.

right.label: Compiles
right.caption_md: `for x in &v` only borrows, so `v` still exists after the loop. It prints `1`, `2` and `3` on separate lines, then `3`.

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank so the loop doubles every element and the program prints `[2, 4, 6]`.
question.general_md: Correct. The loop changes each element, so it needs mutable references: `for x in &mut v`. Then `*x *= 2` doubles the element `x` points at.

wrong_answers.why_md: shared references are read-only, so `*x *= 2` is error E0594 (cannot assign to `*x`, which is behind a `&` reference).
the loop then hands out plain `i32` values, not references, so `*x` is error E0614 (type `{integer}` cannot be dereferenced). And `v` would be moved, so the `println!` couldn't use it either.

screens.heading: No pushing while you loop
screens.text_md:
This is the same E0502 as in the previous lesson, now inside a loop. If `push` grew the buffer, the loop would carry on reading elements from the old, freed one.

The fix is to note what you want to add in a second vector during the loop, then add it to `v` after the loop, when the borrow has ended.

screens.heading: One vector, different kinds of values

coming_from.c: This is a tagged union, like `std::vector<std::variant<int, double, std::string>>`, with `match` playing the role of `std::visit`.
coming_from.go: Instead of a `[]any` and a type switch, you declare an enum. The compiler knows every possible kind, so the `match` must handle them all.
coming_from.java: Instead of a `List<Object>` and `instanceof` checks, you declare an enum of the allowed kinds. The compiler knows the full list, so a missing case is a compile error.
coming_from.js: This is like a TypeScript discriminated union such as `{kind: "int", n: number} | {kind: "text", s: string}` in one array. Rust's `match` checks that every variant is handled.
coming_from.python: A Python list can mix `3`, `"blue"` and `10.12` freely. In Rust, you list the allowed kinds up front in an enum, and `match` makes sure you handle each one.

steps.caption_md: A vector holds values of one type. An **enum** is one type whose variants can carry different kinds of data, so it can stand for "an `i32`, an `f64` or a `String`".
steps.visual_md: Three labelled boxes side by side under the title "enum Cell": `Int(i32)`, `Float(f64)`, `Text(String)`; a bracket under all three labelled "one type: Cell"

steps.caption_md: Every element is a `Cell`, so all three fit in one `Vec<Cell>`. Each element has the same size and records which variant it is, which is what lets Rust store them side by side.
steps.visual_md: A row of three equal-width cells labelled `row: Vec<Cell>`: cell 0 tagged `Int` showing `3`; cell 1 tagged `Text` showing `"blue"`; cell 2 tagged `Float` showing `10.12`

steps.caption_md: The loop borrows each cell in turn, and `match` runs the arm for its variant, binding the data inside to `n`.
steps.visual_md: Cell 0 outlined orange; arm `Cell::Int(n)` highlighted green; output panel: int 3

steps.caption_md: The second cell is a `Text`, so the `Text` arm runs. `s` is a reference to the `String` inside the cell.
steps.visual_md: Cell 1 outlined orange; arm `Cell::Text(s)` highlighted green; output panel: int 3, text blue

steps.caption_md: The third cell runs the `Float` arm. Because `match` must cover every variant, no kind of value in the vector can be forgotten.
steps.visual_md: Cell 2 outlined orange; arm `Cell::Float(f)` highlighted green; output panel: int 3, text blue, float 10.12

screens.heading: Handy vector methods
screens.text_md:
`pop` removes the last element and returns an `Option`, `Some(2)` here, because an empty vector has nothing to pop. `sort` puts the elements in order, and `dedup` removes repeats that sit next to each other, which after sorting means all repeats.

`insert(i, x)` and `remove(i)` work at any position and shift the later elements along. `contains(&x)` and `is_empty()` answer yes or no. This prints `[9, 3, 5] Some(2) 1`, then `true false`.

screens.heading: Totals and the largest value with a loop
screens.text_md:
One loop can compute several results. `total` adds up the elements. `best` starts as `None` and holds the largest element seen so far.

Why an `Option` and not 0? An empty vector has no largest element, and 0 would claim one exists (and would be wrong for a vector of negative numbers). This program prints `19 Some(9)`.

question.general_md: Correct. `sort` gives `[1, 3, 5, 5]`, `dedup` removes the repeated 5 to give `[1, 3, 5]`, and `pop` takes the last element, returning `Some(5)` and leaving `[1, 3]`.

wrong_answers.why_md: `pop` returns an `Option`, because the vector might be empty, so `{:?}` prints it as `Some(5)`.
`pop` removes the element it returns, so 5 is no longer in `v`.
`sort` runs first, so `dedup` sees the two 5s next to each other and keeps one, and the vector is in order.

screens.heading: Reshaping a vector
screens.text_md:
`extend_from_slice` appends copies of several elements at once. `swap(0, 1)` exchanges two positions, `reverse` flips the order and `truncate(3)` keeps only the first 3. `join("+")` glues text elements into one `String`: `gold+blue+red`. `clear` removes everything.

`insert`, `remove` and `swap` panic, like `v[i]`, if a position is out of range (`insert` also accepts `len()`, meaning "at the end"). Check positions that come from outside first.

question.prompt_md: Why does screen 5 wrap `3`, `10.12` and `"blue"` in an enum `Cell` instead of putting them in a vector directly?

options.text_md: All elements of a `Vec` have one type, and `Cell` is that one type: each element records which variant it is.
Enums make `push` faster than storing the values directly.
With an enum, the vector can later hold values of any type, like a Python list.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Rust needs one element type to know the size of every element. `Cell` is one type with three variants, and `match` handles each variant.
Not quite. The enum is about types, not speed. `vec![3, 10.12]` doesn't compile at all, because the elements have different types (E0308).
Not quite. A `Vec<Cell>` holds only the three variants listed in `Cell`. Adding a `bool` would need a new variant, and then every `match` on `Cell` must handle it.

summary: `for x in &v` reads each element through a shared reference; `for x in &mut v` changes elements in place, writing `*x` to reach each value.
`for x in v` moves the elements out and uses the vector up, so `v` can't be used afterwards (E0382).
You can't `push` to a vector while a loop is borrowing it (E0502): collect the changes and apply them after the loop.
An enum lets one `Vec` hold different kinds of values, and `match` handles every kind.
`pop` and `get` return `Option`, because a vector can be empty or too short; `sort`, `dedup`, `insert`, `remove`, `swap`, `reverse`, `truncate`, `extend_from_slice`, `join` and `clear` reshape it.

lessons.title: Creating and updating strings
lessons.book_section: 8.2 Storing UTF-8 Encoded Text with Strings → Defining Strings, Creating a New String, Updating a String
lessons.objective_md: Create a `String` in several ways, grow it with `push_str` and `push`, join strings with `+` (and say which operand is moved) or with `format!`, and read errors E0308 and E0382 caused by `+`.

screens.heading: A `String` is a growable buffer of UTF-8 bytes
screens.text_md:
A `String` is built as a wrapper around a `Vec<u8>`: an owned, growable buffer of bytes, with the promise that the bytes are always valid **UTF-8** text. That's why it has a length and a capacity, like a vector.

A `&str` is a borrowed view of UTF-8 bytes owned by something else: part of `s` here, or text built into the program for a literal. Functions that only read text usually take `&str`. This prints `hello hel`.

screens.heading: Ways to make a `String`
screens.text_md:
`String::new()` makes an empty string. `String::from("hi")` and `"hi".to_string()` both copy a literal into a new owned `String`; pick whichever reads better. `to_string` works on any value that can be printed with `{}`, so `5.to_string()` gives `"5"`.

`String::with_capacity(10)` is empty too, but reserves room for at least 10 bytes, so the first pushes don't need a bigger buffer. Any UTF-8 text works, in any script: this prints `[] hi hi [] नमस्ते`.

steps.caption_md: `s` owns 3 bytes: `foo`. It's `mut` because the next lines change it.
steps.visual_md: Stack box `s` (String: ptr ●, len 3, cap 3) with an orange arrow to heap cells `f` `o` `o`

steps.caption_md: `extra` is a string literal: a `&str` pointing at text stored in the program itself.
steps.visual_md: Second stack box `extra` (&str: ptr ●, len 3) with a blue arrow to a box labelled "in the program" holding `b` `a` `r`

steps.caption_md: `push_str` copies the bytes of a `&str` onto the end of `s`. It takes a `&str` so that it only borrows the text: `extra` is still usable afterwards.
steps.visual_md: Heap cells of `s` now `f` `o` `o` `b` `a` `r`, the last three highlighted; `s` shows len 6; `extra` and its arrow unchanged

steps.caption_md: `push` adds a single `char`, written in single quotes: `'!'`. Like a vector, `s` gets a bigger buffer whenever it runs out of room.
steps.visual_md: Heap cells `f` `o` `o` `b` `a` `r` `!`, the `!` highlighted; `s` shows len 7

steps.caption_md: Both strings can be printed: `foobar! bar`.
steps.visual_md: Same as step 4; output panel: foobar! bar

screens.heading: `+` takes the left string
screens.text_md: `+` on strings calls a method that looks like `fn add(self, s: &str) -> String`. Its first parameter is `self`, not `&self`, and its second is a `&str`.

coming_from.c: It's like `std::move(s1) + s2` in C++: the left string's buffer is reused. Rust makes the move automatic and checked: using `s1` afterwards is a compile error.
coming_from.go: Go strings are immutable and `+` makes a new one. Rust's `+` appends to the left `String`'s own buffer and moves it, much like writing into a `strings.Builder`.
coming_from.java: Java and C# strings are immutable, and `+` copies into a new one. A Rust `String` is mutable, like a `StringBuilder`, and `+` appends to the left one and takes it over.
coming_from.js: In JavaScript, `a + b` makes a new string and both stay usable. Rust's `+` consumes the left `String` and appends to it; use `format!` if you want to keep both.
coming_from.python: Python's `a + b` builds a brand-new string and leaves both alone. Rust's `s1 + &s2` reuses `s1`'s buffer instead, so `s1` is used up.

steps.caption_md: Two strings, two owners.
steps.visual_md: Stack boxes `s1` and `s2`, each with an orange "owner" arrow to its own heap text: `Hello, ` and `world!`

steps.caption_md: `&s2` is a `&String`, but `add` wants a `&str`. Rust converts it automatically with **deref coercion**: the `&String` becomes a `&str` view of all of `s2`'s text.
steps.visual_md: A label `&s2: &String` above the `+`, with an arrow to a second label `&str` (the whole of `s2`'s text)

steps.caption_md: Because `add` takes `self`, `s1` is **moved** into it. `add` appends a copy of `s2`'s text to that buffer (growing it if needed) and returns it, and `s3` now owns it. Reusing `s1`'s buffer saves copying `s1`'s text into a brand-new string.
steps.visual_md: `s1` turns grey and dashed with the tag "moved · unusable"; new stack box `s3` with an orange "owner" arrow to `s1`'s old heap text, which now reads `Hello, world!` (the added part highlighted); a blue "borrow" arrow from the `+` to `s2`'s text; `s2` unchanged

steps.caption_md: `s3` and `s2` can be printed. `s1` can't: it was moved, so using it would be error E0382.
steps.visual_md: Same as step 3; output panel: Hello, world! world!

screens.heading: You can only add a `&str`
screens.text_md:
The left side of `+` is a `String` you give away; the right side is text you only lend. `add` never takes ownership of its right operand, so `s1 + s2` has the wrong type for it.

Add `&s2`, as the compiler suggests. A string literal works too, because it's already a `&str`: `s1 + "!"`.

lessons.book_section: 8.2 Storing UTF-8 Encoded Text with Strings → Indexing into Strings, Slicing Strings, Methods for Iterating Over Strings
lessons.objective_md: Explain why `s[0]` doesn't compile (E0277), tell bytes, `char`s and grapheme clusters apart, slice a string only at character boundaries, and walk a string with `chars`, `bytes` and `char_indices`.

screens.heading: `s[0]` doesn't compile
screens.text_md:
In most languages `s[0]` gives the first letter. Rust refuses, on purpose: a `String` is stored as UTF-8 bytes, and one letter can take several bytes. A byte index could land in the middle of a letter.

So Rust makes you choose what you mean: bytes, characters or a range of bytes. (The `...` line marks where the compiler also lists, with paths into your Rust installation, which types *can* be used as indexes.)
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0277]: the type `str` cannot be indexed by `{integer}`
   --> src/main.rs:3:15
    |
  3 |     let h = s[0];
    |               ^ string indices are ranges of `usize`
    |
    = help: the trait `SliceIndex<str>` is not implemented for `{integer}`
    = note: you can use `.chars().nth()` or `.bytes().nth()`

...

steps.caption_md: In `"Hola"`, every letter is one byte in UTF-8, so `len()` is 4.
steps.visual_md: A row of 4 byte cells under the label `a`: `72` `111` `108` `97`; above each cell its letter `H` `o` `l` `a`, each letter spanning exactly one cell

steps.caption_md: In `"Здравствуйте"`, every Cyrillic letter takes **two** bytes. 12 letters, so `len()` is 24.
steps.visual_md: A row of byte cells under the label `b`, showing the first 6 of 24: `208` `151` `208` `180` `209` `128`; above them the letters `З` `д` `р`, each spanning two cells, with a bracket "2 bytes"; note "… 24 bytes in all"

steps.caption_md: The program prints `4 24`. **`len()` counts bytes, not letters.** Finding the fifth letter would mean walking the bytes from the start, so it couldn't be the instant lookup people expect from `[i]` either.
steps.visual_md: Both rows as before; output panel: 4 24

screens.heading: Three ways to see the same text
screens.text_md:
The same text can be read three ways. As **bytes**: 18. As **`char`s**, Unicode scalar values: 6, and two of them are vowel signs that only make sense attached to a letter. As **grapheme clusters**, what a reader would call letters: 4.

The standard library gives you bytes and `char`s; grapheme clusters need an extra crate. This program counts the `char`s with a loop and prints `18 6`.

coming_from.c: Like a `std::string` holding UTF-8, `len()` is the number of bytes. The difference: Rust guarantees the bytes are valid UTF-8 and stops you from cutting a character in half.
coming_from.go: Very close to Go: strings are UTF-8 bytes, `len` counts bytes, and `for _, r := range s` gives runes, like Rust's `chars()`. The difference: Rust has no `s[i]` byte indexing; use `s.bytes()` instead.
coming_from.java: A Java or C# `char` is a 16-bit UTF-16 unit, so some characters need two. A Rust `char` is always a whole Unicode scalar value (4 bytes in memory), and a `String` stores UTF-8 bytes.
coming_from.js: JavaScript strings are UTF-16, so `"😻".length` is 2 and `s[0]` can return half of an emoji. Rust's `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes, and `chars()` always gives whole characters.
coming_from.python: Python's `len(s)` and `s[i]` count code points, which are Rust's `char`s. Rust's `len()` counts bytes instead, and there is no `s[i]`: use `s.chars()` to walk the code points.

question.prompt_md: `ñ` takes 2 bytes in UTF-8. What does `String::from("añb").len()` return?

explanations.text_md: Not quite. 3 is the number of `char`s, which you'd get by counting `s.chars()`. `len()` counts bytes.
Correct. `a` is 1 byte, `ñ` is 2 and `b` is 1: 4 bytes.
Not quite. UTF-8 uses only as many bytes as each character needs (1 for `a` and `b`); it isn't a fixed 2 bytes per character.
Not quite. `len()` on a `String` is fine; it's indexing with one number, `s[i]`, that doesn't compile.

screens.heading: Looping over chars, bytes and positions
screens.text_md:
To loop over a string, say which view you want. `chars()` gives each `char`: `a`, `ñ`, `b`. `bytes()` gives each raw byte as a `u8`: `97 195 177 98`, so `ñ` shows up as two numbers.

`char_indices()` gives each `char` together with the **byte position** where it starts: `0:a 1:ñ 3:b`. `ñ` starts at byte 1 and takes two bytes, so `b` starts at byte 3. Those positions are always safe places to slice.

screens.heading: A slice takes a byte range
screens.text_md:
Instead of one index, you can ask for a range of bytes, as you did with string slices in Chapter 4. `&hello[0..4]` is a `&str` holding bytes 0 to 3.

Each Cyrillic letter here takes 2 bytes, so those 4 bytes are exactly the first two letters, and the program prints `Зд`. The range is in bytes, not letters: `0..2` would give only `З`.

screens.heading: A slice inside a character panics
screens.text_md:
Both ends of a range must fall on a **character boundary**, where one `char` ends and the next begins. The compiler can't check that, because the text could come from anywhere at run time, so the slice is checked when it runs and the program panics if it would cut a character in half.

Use ranges on strings with care, and get positions from `char_indices` when the text isn't plain ASCII.

annotations.note_md: line 3: the range ends after byte 0, which is only the first half of `З`.
line 3: `З` occupies bytes 0 and 1, so a valid range must end at 0 or 2.

Correct. It compiles, then panics with "end byte index 1 is not a char boundary". Only `s[0]`, with a single number, is a compile error (E0277).

screens.heading: Finding safe positions
screens.text_md:
`is_char_boundary(i)` tells you whether byte position `i` is safe to slice at: byte 1 is inside `З`, byte 2 is where `д` begins.

`char_indices` only ever gives you safe positions. `first_n` uses them to cut after `n` characters, and returns the whole string if it's shorter, so it can never panic. This prints `false true`, then `Здр`, then `hi`.

screens.heading: Splitting and trimming
screens.text_md:
These methods all cut at character boundaries for you, so they never panic. `split(',')` cuts at every comma and keeps empty parts: `[red][green][][blue]`. `lines()` cuts at line breaks, and `split_whitespace()` gives the words.

`strip_prefix` returns `Some(rest)` if the text starts with the prefix, else `None`, so `if let` handles both cases. `trim_start` and `trim_end` remove spaces from one side only: `[hi  ] [  hi]`.

question.general_md: Correct. `char_indices` gives the byte position where each `char` starts. `é` starts at byte 3 and takes bytes 3 and 4, so `!` starts at byte 5.

wrong_answers.why_md: that counts characters, not bytes. `é` takes two bytes, so the next position is 5.
`char_indices` gives each `char` once, at the byte where it starts, never half of one.
byte positions start at 0, like vector indexes.

summary: `s[0]` doesn't compile (E0277): a `String` stores UTF-8 bytes, and one character can take 1 to 4 bytes.
`len()` counts bytes. The same text can be seen as bytes, `char`s (Unicode scalar values) or grapheme clusters; the standard library gives you the first two.
`&s[a..b]` slices by byte position; if either end falls inside a character, the program panics at run time.
Use `chars()`, `bytes()` or `char_indices()` to walk a string; `char_indices` and `is_char_boundary` give positions that are safe to slice at.
`split`, `lines`, `split_whitespace`, `strip_prefix`, `trim_start` and `trim_end` cut text at safe boundaries for you.

lessons.title: Hash maps
lessons.book_section: 8.3 Storing Keys with Associated Values in Hash Maps → Creating a New Hash Map, Accessing Values in a Hash Map, Managing Ownership in Hash Maps
lessons.objective_md: Create a `HashMap`, insert pairs and read values with `get` (handling a missing key), say what happens to a `String` you insert, and print a map's contents in a fixed order.

coming_from.c: `HashMap<K, V>` is Rust's `std::unordered_map`. One difference: there's no `map[key]` that inserts a default; reading a missing key gives `None`.
coming_from.go: `HashMap<K, V>` is like Go's `map[K]V`, and as in Go, the iteration order is not fixed. Reading a missing key gives `None` instead of a zero value.
coming_from.java: `HashMap<K, V>` works like Java's `HashMap` or C#'s `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`: hashed buckets, no guaranteed order, one key type and one value type.
coming_from.js: A `HashMap<K, V>` is like a JavaScript `Map`, but it does **not** keep insertion order. Keys and values each have one fixed type.
coming_from.python: A `HashMap` is like a Python `dict`, with one big difference: a `dict` remembers insertion order, and a `HashMap` doesn't. All keys must have one type, and all values one type.

steps.caption_md: A **hash map** stores pairs: a **key** and its **value**. Instead of positions 0, 1, 2 like a vector, you find a value by its key. The pairs live in a table of slots called **buckets**.
steps.visual_md: Stack box `scores` (HashMap) with an arrow to a heap box "table" with 8 empty bucket rows numbered 0 to 7

steps.caption_md: To insert, Rust runs the key through a **hash function**, which turns it into a number; that number picks the bucket. The default hash function, SipHash, is a little slower than some but resists attacks that feed it colliding keys.
steps.visual_md: A small box "hash(\"Blue\") → 5" between the code and the table, with an arrow to bucket 5; bucket 5 now shows `"Blue"` → `10`

steps.caption_md: `"Yellow"` hashes to a different bucket. To look a key up later, Rust hashes it again and checks only the buckets that number points to, so a lookup doesn't scan every pair.
steps.visual_md: The hash box now reads "hash(\"Yellow\") → 2", with an arrow to bucket 2; bucket 2 shows `"Yellow"` → `50`; bucket 5 still shows `"Blue"` → `10`

steps.caption_md: `len()` counts the pairs: `2 teams`. Where a pair lands depends on its hash, not on when you inserted it, so a hash map has no meaningful order.
steps.visual_md: Same table; output panel: 2 teams; footnote under the table: "Bucket numbers here are made up. Real ones differ from run to run."

screens.heading: Creating a hash map
screens.text_md:
Hash maps are used less often than vectors and strings, so they aren't brought into scope automatically, and there's no `vec!`-style macro to build one. You bring the type in with `use std::collections::HashMap;` and start from `HashMap::new()`.

Every key has one type and every value has one type: here `String` keys and `u32` values. Rust can usually infer both from the first `insert`, so the annotation is optional. This prints `2`.

screens.heading: Reading values with `get`
screens.text_md:
`get` returns an `Option<&V>`: `Some(&10)` for `"Blue"`, `None` for a key that isn't there. `.copied()` turns the `&10` into a plain `10`, and `.unwrap_or(0)` picks 0 when the key is missing. You can look up a `String` key with a plain `"Blue"`, without building a `String`.

`contains_key` answers yes or no. `remove` takes the pair out and returns its value as an `Option`. This prints `10 0`, then `true`, then `Some(50) 1`.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `get` returns an `Option`, and `None` means the key isn't in the map.
Not quite. That's Go's behaviour (a zero value). `get` returns an `Option`; you get 0 only if you ask for it with `.copied().unwrap_or(0)`.
Not quite. `Some` means the key was found. `"Red"` was never inserted, so there's no value to wrap.
Not quite. `get` never panics on a missing key; returning `None` is how it reports one.

screens.heading: Inserting a `String` moves it
screens.text_md:
A map owns its keys and values. Values like `10` are `Copy`, so the map gets a copy and nothing is lost. A `String` is moved into the map, exactly like passing it to a function that takes ownership.

The map needs ownership so its keys can't change or disappear behind its back: a changed key would sit in the wrong bucket.

screens.heading: Keep the key: clone it or lend it
screens.text_md:
Two ways to keep using `name`. `owned` gets a **clone**: its own copy of the text, independent of `name`. `borrowed` stores a `&str` key instead, so nothing moves: the map only points at `name`'s text.

A map of references borrows what it points at, so `name` must stay alive and unchanged for as long as `borrowed` is used (Chapter 10 explains how Rust checks this). This prints `Blue Some(10) Some(20)`.

left.caption_md: `for (name, score) in &scores` visits every pair, borrowing each key and value, but in no fixed order: one run might print `Blue` first, the next run `Green` first.

right.label: Sorted, the same every time

explanations.text_md: Not quite. That's true of Python's `dict` and JavaScript's `Map`, but not of Rust's `HashMap`. Pairs come out in an order that depends on the hashes and can change from run to run.
Correct. The order is arbitrary. Sort the keys first whenever the order matters.

`get(&key)` returns `Option<&V>`: `None` for a missing key, never a panic. `.copied().unwrap_or(0)` turns it into a plain value with a default.
`contains_key` checks for a key, `remove` takes a pair out and returns its value as an `Option`, and `len` counts the pairs.
Inserting a `String` moves it into the map (E0382 if you use it afterwards); `Copy` values are copied. Insert a clone, or a reference that outlives the map, to keep using it.
`for (k, v) in &map` visits pairs in an arbitrary order; sort the keys first when order matters.

screens.heading: Start from a default: `or_default` and `or_insert(Vec::new())`
screens.text_md:
The value can be any type, including a vector. `or_insert(Vec::new())` starts a missing key with an empty vector, then returns a `&mut` to the vector so you can `push`. This groups words by length. (An empty `Vec::new()` allocates nothing, so making one that isn't used costs almost nothing.)

`or_default()` inserts the type's default value: 0 for numbers, an empty `String` or `Vec`. This prints `Some(["fig", "yam"]) Some(2)`.

screens.heading: Change an existing value with `get_mut`
screens.text_md:
`get_mut` returns an `Option<&mut V>`: a mutable reference to the value if the key exists, `None` if it doesn't. `"Blue"` goes from 10 to 15; `"Red"` is missing, so nothing happens.

Unlike `entry`, `get_mut` never adds a key. Use it when a missing key should be left alone (or reported), and `entry` when a missing key should start from a default. This prints `Some(15) false`.

screens.heading: `HashSet`: keys without values
screens.text_md:
A **`HashSet`** stores each value at most once, using the same hashed buckets as a map, but with no value attached. `insert` returns `true` if the value was new and `false` if it was already there, which makes "have I seen this before?" a single call.

`contains`, `remove` and `len` work like a map's, and the iteration order is arbitrary here too. This prints `true`, `true`, `false`, then `2 true`, then `1`.

problems.title: Make a number list
problems.description_md:
Write two functions that each build a brand-new `Vec<i32>` and hand it to the caller. They practise the two ways Chapter 8 creates a vector (Book ch. 8.1, "Creating a New Vector").

- `number_list(first, second)` returns a vector of exactly three elements, in this order: `first`, `second`, `first`. Equal arguments still give three elements.
- `filled(value, count)` returns a vector of exactly `count` elements, each equal to `value`. A `count` of 0 gives an empty vector.

Every `i32` is valid for `first`, `second` and `value`. Neither function prints anything. Because each function returns its `Vec` by value, the caller becomes the owner of the new heap buffer.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::number_list(1,2)
Expected:   vec![1,2,1]
The first argument appears at both ends.

Expression: crate::filled(7,3)
Expected:   vec![7,7,7]
Three copies of 7.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `first`, `second` and `value` are any `i32`, including `i32::MIN` and `i32::MAX`.
- `count` is between 0 and 100,000.
hints: Both results are new vectors that the function creates and returns; neither needs an input vector.
The `vec!` macro takes a comma-separated list of elements, and it also has a second form, `vec![value; count]`, that repeats one value.
`number_list` is `vec![first, second, first]`; `filled` is `vec![value; count]`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Write the three elements of `number_list` directly in a `vec!` literal. For `filled`, use the repeat form `vec![value; count]`, which allocates `count` copies of `value` at once (and no buffer at all for `count == 0`).
problems.idiomatic_md: `vec![value; count]` states "count copies of value" in one expression and allocates once. A `Vec::new()` followed by a `push` loop gives the same vector, but it is longer and may reallocate as it grows.

problems.title: Read safely
problems.description_md:
`read(v, index, fallback)` returns the element of `v` at position `index`, or `fallback` when there is no element at that position. It must never panic, whatever the index.

Chapter 8 shows two ways to read an element (Book ch. 8.1, "Reading Elements of Vectors"): indexing with `v[index]`, which panics when the index is out of range, and `v.get(index)`, which returns `Option<&i32>`: `Some` with a reference to the element, or `None`. This problem practises the second one: read the element with `get`, not with `[]`.

- Positions start at 0, so the valid indices are `0..v.len()`. An index equal to the length, or any larger one up to `usize::MAX`, gives `fallback`.
- A present element is returned even when it equals `fallback` or is 0; only a missing element gives `fallback`.
- `v` is borrowed (`&[i32]`; callers pass `&vec`), so the caller still owns its vector after the call and the function must not change it.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::read(&vec![10,20,30],1,-1)
Expected:   20
Index 1 is the second element.

Expression: crate::read(&vec![10,20,30],3,-1)
Expected:   -1
Valid indices are 0, 1 and 2, so index 3 has no element.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `v` has 0 to 100,000 elements; elements and `fallback` are any `i32`.
- `index` is any `usize`.
- The body of `read` uses `get`, with no indexing expression.
hints: Indexing panics on a missing position, so look for a method that reports a missing element instead of panicking.
`v.get(index)` returns `Option<&i32>`; you still need to turn that into a plain `i32`, using the fallback for `None`.
`v.get(index).copied().unwrap_or(fallback)`: `copied` turns the `Option<&i32>` into an `Option<i32>`, and `unwrap_or` supplies the fallback.
problems.solution_approach_md: Call `v.get(index)`. It does the bounds check and returns `None` for any index at or beyond the length, so no comparison with `len` is needed. Copy the referenced `i32` out of the `Option` and fall back to `fallback` for `None`. A `match` with arms `Some(n) => *n` and `None => fallback` does the same thing.
problems.idiomatic_md: `get` returns an optional reference into the vector's buffer. `.copied()` then copies the `i32` out of it, so the result no longer borrows `v`. Taking `&[i32]` rather than `&Vec<i32>` lets callers pass a vector, an array or a slice.

problems.title: Remember before appending
problems.description_md:
`remember(v, n)` takes ownership of a vector, appends `n` to its end, and returns two things: the value that was the first element **before** the push (`None` if the vector was empty), and the updated vector.

The order matters because of a borrowing rule from the Book (ch. 8.1, "Reading Elements of Vectors"): a reference to an element, such as `&v[0]`, cannot still be in use when `v.push(...)` runs, because the push may move the whole buffer to new memory (error E0502). So copy the first value out (an `i32` is `Copy`) into its own variable, then push.

- For an empty vector the first value is `None` and the result vector is just `[n]`.
- Push onto the vector you were given: do not clone the vector or build a new one.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::remember(vec![1],2)
Expected:   (Some(1),vec![1,2])
The first element was 1 before 2 was pushed.

Expression: crate::remember(vec![],7)
Expected:   (None,vec![7])
There was no first element, so the result starts with `None`.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `v` has 0 to 100,000 elements; elements and `n` are any `i32`.
- The body appends with `v.push(n)` and makes no `clone`, `to_vec` or `to_owned` call.
hints: Read the first element before you change the vector, and keep a copy rather than a reference.
`v.get(0)` gives `Option<&i32>` (it is `None` for an empty vector); `.copied()` turns it into an `Option<i32>` that does not borrow `v`.
`let first = v.get(0).copied(); v.push(n); (first, v)`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Store `v.get(0).copied()` in a local variable. It is an `Option<i32>` that owns its value, so the borrow of `v` ends at once. Then `v.push(n)` can borrow `v` mutably, and the function returns the saved value together with the vector.
problems.idiomatic_md: Copying a `Copy` element out of the vector is cheap and ends the shared borrow straight away. Holding a `&i32` across the `push` is exactly what the borrow checker rejects, because the push may reallocate the buffer.

problems.title: Sum borrowed numbers
problems.description_md:
`total(v)` returns the sum of all elements of `v` as an `i64`.

Iterate over the vector with a `for` loop over a shared reference (Book ch. 8.1, "Iterating Over the Values in a Vector"): `for n in v` visits each element as a `&i32` without consuming or changing the vector, and the caller keeps its vector.

- An empty vector sums to 0.
- Widen each element to `i64` before adding it. Two `i32` values can already add up to more than `i32::MAX`, and with up to 100,000 elements the total always fits in an `i64`.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::total(&vec![1,2,3])
Expected:   6
The total is 1 + 2 + 3.

Expression: crate::total(&vec![5,-1,5])
Expected:   9
The total is 5 - 1 + 5.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `v` has 0 to 100,000 elements, each any `i32`.
- Do not use `sum` or other iterator methods; use a `for` loop.
hints: Keep a running total in a `mut` variable, and add one element to it per loop pass.
`for n in v` gives `n: &i32`; dereference it with `*n` and convert it with `as i64` before adding.
`let mut total = 0i64; for n in v { total += *n as i64; } total`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Start an `i64` accumulator at 0. Loop over the borrowed elements, convert each one to `i64` and add it. Return the accumulator.
problems.idiomatic_md: Widening each element before the addition, rather than summing in `i32` and widening at the end, is what keeps the total exact. `for n in v` over `&[i32]` borrows the elements, so nothing is moved out of the caller's vector.

problems.title: Shift each score
problems.description_md:
`shift(scores, delta)` adds `delta` to every score, changing the caller's vector in place. It returns nothing; the caller sees the new values in its own vector.

This practises iterating over mutable references (Book ch. 8.1, "Iterating Over the Values in a Vector"): `for s in scores` over a `&mut [i32]` gives each element as a `&mut i32`, and `*s = ...` writes through it.

- The addition saturates: a result above `i32::MAX` becomes `i32::MAX`, and a result below `i32::MIN` becomes `i32::MIN`. It never panics or wraps around.
- An empty vector stays empty, and a `delta` of 0 leaves every score unchanged.
- The order and the number of elements never change.

Because `shift` borrows the vector mutably, the caller cannot hold a reference to one of its elements across the call (error E0502, Book ch. 8.1).
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: {let mut v=vec![1,2];crate::shift(&mut v,3);v}
Expected:   vec![4,5]
Both scores go up by 3.

Expression: {let mut v=vec![i32::MAX,0];crate::shift(&mut v,1);v}
Expected:   vec![2147483647,1]
The first score is already the largest `i32`, so it stays there.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `scores` has 0 to 100,000 elements; elements and `delta` are any `i32`.
- Callers pass `&mut v` for a `Vec<i32>`.
hints: You need to change each element where it is, so loop over mutable references to the elements.
`for s in scores` gives `s: &mut i32`; read the old value with `*s` and assign the new one with `*s = ...`.
Inside the loop: `*s = s.saturating_add(delta);`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Loop over the mutable slice. For each element compute `saturating_add(delta)` and store it back through the mutable reference. The function returns `()`, so the result is visible only through the caller's vector.
problems.idiomatic_md: Changing elements through `&mut` avoids building a second vector. `saturating_add` states the clamping rule directly, where comparisons against `i32::MAX - delta` are easy to get wrong for negative deltas.

problems.title: Sorted unique numbers
problems.description_md:
`unique(v)` takes ownership of a vector of numbers and returns it sorted in ascending order with every repeated value kept only once.

This practises two common vector methods (Book ch. 8.1 and the `Vec` documentation it links to): `sort` (or `sort_unstable`) puts the elements in order, and `dedup` removes **consecutive** repeats. `dedup` alone is not enough, because equal values are only next to each other once the vector is sorted.

- An empty vector stays empty.
- The result has each distinct input value exactly once, smallest first.
- Change and return the vector you were given; there is no need to allocate another one.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::unique(vec![3,1,2])
Expected:   vec![1,2,3]
No repeats, just sorting.

Expression: crate::unique(vec![5,-1,5])
Expected:   vec![-1,5]
5 appears twice but is kept once.
```
problems.constraints_md: - `v` has 0 to 100,000 elements, each any `i32`.
hints: Two steps: put equal values next to each other, then drop the repeats.
`v.sort_unstable()` orders the numbers; `v.dedup()` then removes each element that equals the one before it.
`v.sort_unstable(); v.dedup(); v`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Sort the owned vector in place, which puts all copies of a value next to each other. Then `dedup` removes every element equal to its predecessor in one pass. Return the same vector.
problems.idiomatic_md: For plain integers, `sort_unstable` is the usual choice: equal `i32`s cannot be told apart, so stability does not matter, and it avoids the extra buffer `sort` uses. Taking `mut v: Vec<i32>` by value lets the function reuse the caller's buffer.

- An empty `text` gives `"[]"`.

problems.title: Consume the left string
problems.description_md:
`combine(left, right)` returns `left`, then a single `:`, then `right`, built with the `+` operator.

The Book (ch. 8.2, "Concatenation with the + Operator or the format! Macro") explains how `+` treats its operands: the left operand must be an owned `String` and is **moved** into the operation, which appends to its buffer and returns it; the right operand is only borrowed as a `&str`. That is why this function takes `left: String` by value and `right: &str` by reference.

- Use `+` with `left` as the left operand: `left + ":" + right`. Do not clone `left`, and do not build a new string with `format!` or `push_str`.
- After the call, the caller's `left` has been moved and can no longer be used, but the caller's `right` is still usable.
- Both parts are copied exactly; either may be empty or contain `:`.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::combine("L".to_string(),"rust")
Expected:   "L:rust".to_string()
Left, colon, right.

Expression: crate::combine(String::new(),"")
Expected:   ":".to_string()
Both parts are empty.
```
problems.constraints_md:

problems.description_md:
`pop_scalar(text)` takes ownership of a `String`, removes its last `char` (one Unicode scalar value), and returns the shortened string together with the removed `char`, or `None` if the string was empty.

One user-visible character may be several scalars: for `"e\u{301}"` (e followed by a combining acute accent) only the accent is removed.

- An empty string comes back empty, paired with `None`.
- A newline, a space or any other scalar is removed like any other.

problems.title: Read text records
problems.description_md:
`records(text)` splits a block of text into lines and cleans each line into an owned `String`. The result has one entry per line, in order.

Use `text.lines()` (Book ch. 8.2, "Methods for Iterating Over Strings", and the `str` documentation). It splits at `\n` and also removes a `\r` just before it (so `\r\n` line endings work). A final line ending does not start an extra empty line, and an empty `text` has no lines at all.

Each line is cleaned like this:

1. trim Unicode whitespace from both ends (`trim`), which includes tabs and the ideographic space U+3000;
2. if the trimmed line starts with `#`, remove that one `#` (`strip_prefix`, which returns an `Option`);
3. trim both ends again, so `"#  pear"` becomes `"pear"`.

Lines that end up empty are kept as `""`. A `#` anywhere other than at the start is ordinary text, and only one leading `#` is removed.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::records("apple\n  # pear \nplum")
Expected:   vec!["apple".to_string(),"pear".to_string(),"plum".to_string()]
The middle line loses its spaces and its `#`.

Expression: crate::records("")
Expected:   Vec::<String>::new()
`lines` yields nothing for an empty string.
```
problems.constraints_md: - `text` is valid UTF-8 of at most 100,000 bytes.
hints: Loop over the lines and push one cleaned, owned `String` per line into a result vector.
`line.trim()` gives a `&str`; `s.strip_prefix('#')` is `Some(rest)` when `s` starts with `#` and `None` otherwise, and `unwrap_or(s)` keeps `s` in the `None` case.
For each `line` in `text.lines()`: `let s = line.trim(); let s = s.strip_prefix('#').unwrap_or(s).trim(); out.push(s.to_string());`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Iterate over `text.lines()`. For each line, trim, remove at most one leading `#` with `strip_prefix`, trim again, and push an owned copy with `to_string`. Every step before the final copy is a borrowed `&str` view into `text`, so only the result strings allocate.
problems.idiomatic_md: `trim` and `strip_prefix` return slices of the original line, so the cleanup copies nothing until `to_string`. `lines` already handles `\r\n` and the final newline, which splitting by hand on `'\n'` would get wrong.

`report(entries)` turns a list of `(name, score)` pairs into a text report with one line per distinct name, sorted by name.

Build a `HashMap<String, u32>` by inserting every pair in order (Book ch. 8.3). The owned names move into the map, and a name that appears again replaces its earlier score, so the **last** score for each name wins. Then produce the report: for each name, a line `name=score` followed by `\n` (including after the last line). An empty input gives an empty string.

Names are compared with Rust's normal `str` ordering, byte by byte: uppercase ASCII letters come before lowercase ones, a prefix comes before longer names that start with it, and `é` comes after `z`.

problems.title: Running totals
problems.description_md:
`prefixes(v)` returns a new vector of running totals: element `i` of the result is the sum of `v[0]` through `v[i]`. The result has the same length as `v`, and an empty input gives an empty result.

Build the result with `Vec::new()` and `push` while walking the borrowed input once with `for n in v` (Book ch. 8.1, "Updating a Vector" and "Iterating Over the Values in a Vector"). Keep one running total and push it after each addition. Recomputing every total from the start would take time proportional to the square of the length.

- The totals are `i64`. Widen each element to `i64` before adding, because totals of `i32` values easily leave the `i32` range. With at most 100,000 elements, every total fits in an `i64`.
- The input is borrowed and stays unchanged. The result is a separate, owned vector that does not borrow the input, so the caller may change its vector afterwards while keeping the totals.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::prefixes(&vec![1,2,3])
Expected:   vec![1,3,6]
1, then 1 + 2, then 1 + 2 + 3.

Expression: crate::prefixes(&vec![5,-1,5])
Expected:   vec![5,4,9]
The total goes 5, 4, 9.
```

- `v` has 0 to 100,000 elements, each any `i32`.
- No `sum` or other iterator methods; use a `for` loop.
hints: One loop is enough: carry the total from one element to the next instead of starting again.
Keep `let mut total = 0i64;` and an output `Vec`; for each `n` in `v`, add `*n as i64` to `total`, then `push` a copy of `total`.
`let mut out = Vec::new(); let mut total = 0i64; for n in v { total += *n as i64; out.push(total); } out`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Create an empty output vector and an `i64` accumulator. For each borrowed element, widen it, add it to the accumulator and push the accumulator's new value (an `i64` is `Copy`, so the pushed value is independent). Return the output vector.
problems.idiomatic_md: A single pass with a carried total is linear. Taking `&[i32]` and returning a fresh `Vec<i64>` keeps input and output separate, so no borrow of `v` outlives the call.

problems.description_md:
`partition(v)` splits the borrowed numbers into two new vectors and returns them as a pair: first all the negative values, then all the other values (zero and positive).

The split is **stable**: inside each vector the values keep the order they had in `v`, and repeated values are all kept. Walk `v` once with `for n in v` and push each value onto one of two vectors created with `Vec::new()` (Book ch. 8.1). Sorting is not allowed, because it would lose the original order.

- 0 is not negative, so it goes into the second vector; -1 goes into the first.
- Either vector may be empty; an empty input gives two empty vectors.
- Every input value appears exactly once in the output, so the two lengths add up to `v.len()`.
- The input is only borrowed and stays unchanged.

problems.title: Merge sorted lists
problems.description_md:
`merge(a, b)` receives two borrowed vectors that are each already sorted in nondecreasing order and returns one new vector that holds every element of both, also in nondecreasing order.

This is the merge step of merge sort, and it needs no sorting at all. Keep one read position in each input and compare the two current elements with indexing (`a[i]`, Book ch. 8.1, "Reading Elements of Vectors"); push the smaller one onto the output (Book ch. 8.1, "Updating a Vector") and move only that position forward. When one input runs out, everything left in the other is already in order and is appended as it is; `extend_from_slice(&a[i..])` copies a whole remaining slice in one call.

- Duplicates are kept: a value that occurs twice in `a` and once in `b` occurs three times in the result, so `merge(a, b).len()` is always `a.len() + b.len()`.
- When the current elements are equal, take the one from `a` first. Because the elements are plain `i32` values, this choice does not change the result, but it keeps the loop simple.
- Either input, or both, may be empty. Both inputs are only borrowed and stay unchanged.
- Calling `sort` or `sort_unstable` is not allowed; the point is to use the order the inputs already have.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::merge(&vec![1,4,9],&vec![2,3,10])
Expected:   vec![1,2,3,4,9,10]
The fronts are compared one pair at a time: 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10.

Expression: crate::merge(&vec![1,2,2],&vec![2,5])
Expected:   vec![1,2,2,2,5]
All three 2s are kept.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `a` and `b` each have 0 to 50,000 elements, any `i32` values, each sorted in nondecreasing order.
- No `sort` or `sort_unstable` call in `merge` (checked by row 13).
- No closures or iterator methods; use `while` loops and indexing.
hints: Both inputs are already in order, so the smallest remaining element is always at the front of what is left of `a` or of `b`; you only ever compare two elements.

Keep `let mut i = 0;` and `let mut j = 0;`. While `i < a.len() && j < b.len()`, push `a[i]` (and advance `i`) if `a[i] <= b[j]`, otherwise push `b[j]` (and advance `j`). The `len` checks keep every index in range.
After the loop at most one input has elements left: `out.extend_from_slice(&a[i..]); out.extend_from_slice(&b[j..]);` appends them (an empty range `&a[a.len()..]` is allowed and adds nothing).
problems.solution_approach_md: Create an empty output vector and two positions starting at 0. While both inputs have elements left, compare `a[i]` with `b[j]`, push the smaller (ties from `a`) and advance its position. Then append the rest of `a` from `i` and the rest of `b` from `j`. Each element is visited once, so the work is proportional to `a.len() + b.len()`.
problems.idiomatic_md: Indexing is safe here because every `a[i]` sits behind an `i < a.len()` check in the loop condition. Taking `&[i32]` instead of `&Vec<i32>` accepts any borrowed run of `i32` values, and a `&vec![...]` argument coerces to it automatically. `extend_from_slice` copies the leftover tail in one call instead of a second loop.

A spreadsheet row is a `Vec<Cell>`, where each cell is a number, a piece of text or empty. One enum lets a single vector hold all three kinds of value (Book ch. 8.1, "Using an Enum to Store Multiple Types").

problems.description_md:
An editor keeps two versions of each draft: a revised copy that gets an exclamation mark, and an untouched copy of the original. `editions(texts)` borrows a list of drafts and returns, for each draft in order, the pair `(revised, original)`.

- `revised` is the draft followed by one `!` (`push('!')` on a copy, Book ch. 8.2, "Updating a String").
- `original` is an exact copy of the draft.

Both strings in every pair, and the caller's list itself, must be independent owners of their text: changing any one of them afterwards must not change the others. A `String` owns its heap bytes, so `clone` makes a real copy (Book ch. 8.2, "Creating a New String"; Chapter 4, "Variables and Data Interacting with Clone"). The input is borrowed as `&[String]` and stays unchanged; the result is a new `Vec` built with `push`.

- An empty draft gives `("!", "")`.
- Repeated drafts give repeated pairs; an empty list gives an empty result.


problems.title: Scalar chunking
problems.description_md:
`chunks(text, size)` cuts `text` into consecutive pieces of `size` Unicode scalar values (Rust `char`s) each and returns them as owned `String`s, in order. The last piece holds whatever is left and may be shorter; no piece is ever empty.

A Rust string is UTF-8, so one scalar takes 1 to 4 bytes and a byte position is not a scalar position (Book ch. 8.2, "Indexing into Strings"). Slicing `&text[start..end]` panics unless both ends are scalar boundaries (Book ch. 8.2, "Slicing Strings"). `text.char_indices()` gives each scalar together with the byte offset where it starts, which is always a safe place to cut (Book ch. 8.2, "Methods for Iterating Over Strings").

- `size == 0` returns an empty vector (there is no way to make progress with empty pieces).
- Empty text returns an empty vector for every size.
- A size of at least the scalar count returns the whole text as one piece (`usize::MAX` included).
- Scalars are counted, not graphemes: a combining mark such as U+0301 counts on its own and may land in a different piece from the letter before it. Whitespace, NUL and every other scalar count like any other.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::chunks("rustacean",4)
Expected:   vec!["rust".to_string(),"acea".to_string(),"n".to_string()]
Nine scalars make two full pieces and one left over.

Expression: crate::chunks("é東😀a",2)
Expected:   vec!["é東".to_string(),"😀a".to_string()]
Two scalars per piece, however many bytes each takes.
```
problems.constraints_md: - `text` is valid UTF-8 of at most 100,000 bytes; `size` is any `usize`.
hints: A piece ends just before the scalar that would make it one too long, so you need to know where each scalar starts in bytes, not just the scalars themselves.

Loop over `text.char_indices()`, counting scalars in the current piece. When the count reaches `size` at byte offset `i`, push `text[start..i].to_string()`, then set `start = i` and the count to 0. Handle `size == 0` before the loop.
After the loop, `if start < text.len() { out.push(text[start..].to_string()); }` adds the last, possibly shorter piece and never an empty one.
problems.solution_approach_md: Return an empty vector at once when `size` is 0. Otherwise walk `char_indices`, keeping the byte offset where the current piece starts and how many scalars it holds. Before counting a scalar, if the piece is already full, cut at that scalar's byte offset. After the loop, push the remainder if it is non-empty. Every cut is at an offset that `char_indices` produced, so no slice can panic.
problems.idiomatic_md: Slicing at offsets from `char_indices` is the safe way to cut UTF-8 text: the offsets are guaranteed scalar boundaries. Collecting `chars()` into a fresh `String` per piece also works; slicing just copies each piece's bytes in one go.

For each case draw `t = text()`, then `k = pick(7)`; the size is `k` when `k < 6` and `usize::MAX` when `k == 6`. Call `crate::chunks(t, size)` and compare with the oracle: no pieces when the size is 0 or `t` is empty; otherwise `t`'s scalars split into consecutive groups of `size`, the last group possibly shorter. Use the common generator, seed `0x08000017`, exactly 300 cases.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Insert at scalar position
problems.description_md:
`insert_scalar(text, position, ch)` returns a copy of `text` with `ch` inserted so that it becomes the scalar at index `position` (counting Unicode scalar values from 0), or `None` when there is no such place.

- `position == 0` puts `ch` first; `position` equal to the number of scalars puts it at the end.
- Any larger `position` returns `None` (including `usize::MAX`).
- `text` itself is borrowed and unchanged; the result is a new `String`.

`String::insert(idx, ch)` takes a **byte** index and panics unless `idx` is a scalar boundary (Book ch. 8.2, "Updating a String" and "Slicing Strings"). Translate the scalar position to a byte offset with `char_indices`, which yields each scalar's starting byte (Book ch. 8.2, "Methods for Iterating Over Strings"). The scalars of `text` are counted as they are: a combining mark such as U+0301 is its own scalar, so inserting at the position after `e` puts `ch` between the `e` and its accent.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::insert_scalar("rust",1,'-')
Expected:   Some("r-ust".to_string())
`-` goes after the first scalar.

Expression: crate::insert_scalar("é東",1,'😀')
Expected:   Some("é😀東".to_string())
The emoji goes between `é` and `東`.
```
problems.constraints_md: - `text` is valid UTF-8 of at most 100,000 bytes; `position` is any `usize`; `ch` is any `char`.
hints: Find the byte offset where scalar number `position` starts. If the text has exactly `position` scalars, the offset is the end, `text.len()`.
Walk `text.char_indices()` with a counter. When the counter equals `position`, the current byte index is the place to insert; after the loop, the counter is the scalar count.
At the found offset `i`: `let mut out = text.to_string(); out.insert(i, ch); return Some(out);`. After the loop: if `count == position`, `push(ch)` onto a copy and return it; otherwise return `None`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Count scalars while walking `char_indices`. When the count reaches `position`, copy the text into a `String`, `insert` `ch` at that scalar's byte offset and return it. If the loop ends first, the count is the number of scalars: `position` equal to it means appending with `push`, and anything larger means `None`.
problems.idiomatic_md: `insert` and `push` both take a `char` and encode it as UTF-8 for you; only the index must be in bytes. Using offsets from `char_indices` guarantees `insert` never panics, and the early `return` stops scanning as soon as the place is found.

For each case draw `t = text()`, then `k = pick(4)`: the position is the scalar count of `t` when `k == 0`, the scalar count plus 1 when `k == 1`, and otherwise a further `pick(26)`. Then draw `ch` as one scalar of the `text()` alphabet with `pick(12)`. Call `crate::insert_scalar(t, position, ch)` and compare with the oracle: `Some` of the first `position` scalars of `t`, then `ch`, then the rest, when `position` is at most the scalar count; otherwise `None`. Use the common generator, seed `0x08000018`, exactly 300 cases.

Rows 2, 11 and 12 catch using `position` as a byte index (`insert` panics on row 2, inside `é`). Rows 4 and 6 catch rejecting the end position. Row 12 is the largest input; the task is one linear scan, so no slower approach is targeted.

problems.title: Word frequency table
problems.description_md:
`frequencies(text)` counts how many times each word occurs in `text` and returns one `(word, count)` pair per distinct word, sorted by word.

A word is what `text.split_whitespace()` yields: a maximal run of non-whitespace scalars, where whitespace is Unicode whitespace (space, tab, newline, the ideographic space U+3000 and others). Words compare exactly: case matters, punctuation stays attached, and no Unicode normalization is applied (`é` and `e` + U+0301 are different words).

Count with a `HashMap<String, usize>` and the entry API, exactly as the Book's word-count example does: `*map.entry(word.to_string()).or_insert(0) += 1` (Book ch. 8.3, "Updating a Value Based on the Old Value"). The map owns its `String` keys (Book ch. 8.3, "Hash Maps and Ownership"), so the result does not borrow `text`.

Iterating over a map visits its entries in an arbitrary order (Book ch. 8.3, "Accessing Values in a Hash Map"). Move the pairs into a `Vec` with a `for` loop and `sort` it: words are unique, so the pairs end up ordered by word under Rust's byte-wise `str` ordering (uppercase ASCII before lowercase, a prefix before longer words, `é` after every ASCII letter, CJK after that).
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::frequencies("the cat the hat")
Expected:   vec![("cat".to_string(),1),("hat".to_string(),1),("the".to_string(),2)]
`the` occurs twice; the list is in word order.

Expression: crate::frequencies("")
Expected:   vec![]
Nothing to count.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `text` is valid UTF-8 of at most 100,000 bytes.
- No closures or iterator methods; gather the pairs with a `for` loop and sort them with `sort`.
hints: Two phases: count every word in a map, then turn the map into a sorted list. The map's own order is not usable.
`for word in text.split_whitespace() { *counts.entry(word.to_string()).or_insert(0) += 1; }` creates a 0 for a new word and adds 1 every time.
`for (word, n) in counts { out.push((word, n)); }` moves the owned keys out of the map; then `out.sort();` and return `out`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Create an empty `HashMap`. For each word slice, `entry(word.to_string())` finds or creates its counter and `or_insert(0)` returns `&mut usize`, which is incremented. Then consume the map in a `for` loop, pushing each `(String, usize)` into a vector, and sort the vector.
problems.idiomatic_md: `entry(...).or_insert(0)` handles the first and the later occurrences of a word with one lookup and no `if`. Consuming the map with `for (word, n) in counts` moves the `String` keys into the result instead of cloning them.

problems.title: First repeated scalar
problems.description_md:
`first_repeat(text)` reads `text` from left to right, one Unicode scalar value (`char`) at a time, and returns the first scalar that has already appeared earlier, or `None` if every scalar is different.

"First" means the earliest **second occurrence**: in `abcba` the answer is `b` (seen again at index 3), not `a` (seen again only at index 4).

Keep the scalars seen so far in a `HashSet<char>` (L8.6). `insert` returns `false` when the value was already in the set, which is exactly the moment to stop. Walk the text with `chars()` (Book ch. 8.2, "Methods for Iterating Over Strings").

- Comparison is exact scalar equality: `a` and `A` differ, and `é` (U+00E9) differs from `e` followed by U+0301. A combining mark is a scalar of its own and can itself be the answer.
- Spaces, tabs, newlines, U+3000 and NUL are scalars like any other.
- Empty text returns `None`.

```text

Expected:   Some('o')
The second `o` is the first repeat.

Expression: crate::first_repeat("rust")
Expected:   None
Every scalar is new.
```

Create `let mut seen = HashSet::new();` and loop `for c in text.chars()`. `seen.insert(c)` adds `c` and tells you whether it was new.
`if !seen.insert(c) { return Some(c); }` inside the loop, and `None` after it.
problems.solution_approach_md: Scan the scalars in order, inserting each into a set. The first time `insert` reports that the scalar was already present, return it. If the scan ends, no scalar repeated.
problems.idiomatic_md: Using the `bool` from `insert` combines the membership test and the update into one hash lookup. The early `return` stops at the first repeat, so the rest of the text is never read. A `HashSet<char>` stores 4-byte scalars, independent of how many bytes each takes in UTF-8.

problems.title: Stable unique names
problems.description_md:
`stable_unique(names)` takes ownership of a list of names and returns the distinct names in the order of their **first** appearance. Later copies of a name are dropped.

A `HashSet` (L8.6) answers "have I already kept this name?" in constant expected time, but iterating over the set would visit the names in an arbitrary order. So keep two collections: the set for membership, and an output `Vec` that receives each name the first time it appears (Book ch. 8.1, "Updating a Vector"). `insert` on the set returns `true` exactly when the value was new.

Both collections need an owned `String`: the vector keeps the name you return, and the set keeps its own copy, made with `clone` (Chapter 4). Because `names` is taken by value, the loop `for name in names` moves each `String` out of it, so the copy you push to the result costs nothing extra.

- Names compare exactly: case, whitespace and Unicode form all matter (`é` differs from `e` + U+0301, `"a"` differs from `" a"`).
- The empty name `""` is a valid name.
- An empty list returns an empty list.

problems.description_md:
`positions(text)` lists, for each distinct word of `text`, every position at which it occurs. Positions count words, not bytes: the first word is at position 0, the next at 1, and so on.

The entry API creates an empty vector the first time a word is seen and returns a mutable reference to it every time, so one line appends the position: `map.entry(word.to_string()).or_default().push(i)` (Book ch. 8.3, "Updating a Hash Map"; `or_default()` inserts `Vec::new()` for a missing key).

Return the groups as `(word, positions)` pairs sorted by word under Rust's byte-wise `str` ordering. The map's own iteration order is arbitrary, so gather the pairs into a `Vec` and `sort` it. Each list of positions is already ascending, because positions are appended in reading order.

`for (word, list) in groups { out.push((word, list)); } out.sort();` and return `out`. Words are unique, so sorting compares only the words.

problems.title: Stock reconciliation
problems.description_md:
A warehouse log is a list of `(item name, change)` pairs: a positive change adds stock, a negative one removes it. `reconcile(changes)` takes ownership of the log and returns the net change for each distinct item, as `(name, total)` pairs sorted by name.

Accumulate in a `HashMap<String, i64>` with the entry API: `*map.entry(name).or_insert(0) += change as i64` (Book ch. 8.3, "Updating a Value Based on the Old Value"). Because the log is owned, each `String` name can be moved straight into the map as its key, with no copy (Book ch. 8.3, "Hash Maps and Ownership").

- Totals are `i64`: widen each `i32` change before adding, because a few large changes overflow `i32`. With at most 100,000 changes every total fits in `i64`.
- An item whose changes cancel out keeps its entry with total 0; so does an item that only ever had a change of 0.
- Names compare exactly (case, spaces and Unicode form matter); the empty name is a valid name.
- Sort the result by name with Rust's byte-wise `str` ordering; the map's iteration order is arbitrary. An empty log gives an empty result.

```text

Expected:   vec![("bolt".to_string(),5),("nut".to_string(),3)]

Expected:   vec![]
```

`for (name, change) in changes { *totals.entry(name).or_insert(0i64) += change as i64; }` moves each name into the map and widens before adding.
`for (name, total) in totals { out.push((name, total)); } out.sort();` and return `out`.
