problems.title: Median and mode
problems.description_md:
This is the first exercise at the end of Book ch. 8: given a list of integers, find the median and the mode. `statistics(v)` takes ownership of the list and returns `Some((median, mode))`, or `None` for an empty list.

- **Median.** Sort the list (`sort`, Book ch. 8.1 and L8.2) and take the element at index `(len - 1) / 2`. For an odd length this is the middle element; for an even length it is the **lower** of the two middle elements. No averaging is done, so the median is always one of the input values and nothing can overflow.
- **Mode.** The value that occurs most often. Count occurrences in a `HashMap<i32, usize>` with `*counts.entry(n).or_insert(0) += 1` (Book ch. 8.3, "Updating a Value Based on the Old Value"). When several values share the highest count, the mode is the **smallest** of them.

The map visits its entries in an arbitrary order, so the tie rule must not depend on that order: while scanning the counts, replace the current best when a count is higher, or equal with a smaller value. Because the list is owned, it may be sorted in place.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::statistics(vec![1,2,3])
Expected:   Some((2,1))
Every value occurs once, so the smallest, 1, is the mode.

Expression: crate::statistics(vec![5,-1,5])
Expected:   Some((5,5))
Sorted: -1, 5, 5.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `v` has 0 to 100,000 elements, each any `i32`.
- No closures or iterator methods (`max_by_key`, `sum` and the like); use `for` loops.
hints: Handle the empty list first. The median needs the values in order; the mode needs a count per distinct value. They are two separate passes.
Declare the parameter `mut v`, call `v.sort()`, and read `v[(v.len() - 1) / 2]`. Then fill a `HashMap` with `entry(*n).or_insert(0)` for each `n` in `&v`.
Start with `best = v[0]` and `best_count = 0`. For each `(n, c)` in the map: `if c > best_count || (c == best_count && n < best) { best = n; best_count = c; }`. Return `Some((median, best))`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Return `None` for an empty list. Otherwise sort the owned vector and read the lower median by index. Count every value with the entry API. Scan the counts once, keeping the value with the highest count and, among equal counts, the smaller value; because that rule picks one answer whatever order the map yields, the result is deterministic.
problems.idiomatic_md: Sorting the owned `Vec` in place avoids a copy, and `(len - 1) / 2` gives the lower median without any arithmetic on the values themselves. Writing the tie-break into the comparison (`c == best_count && n < best`) is what makes a result computed from a `HashMap` reproducible.

Call `crate::statistics(v)` and compare with the oracle: `None` when empty; otherwise the element at index `(len - 1) / 2` of the sorted list, and the smallest of the values with the highest count. Use the common generator, seed `0x0800001e`, exactly 300 cases.

problems.title: Unicode run encoding
problems.description_md:
Run-length encoding replaces each run of equal neighbours by one value and a count. `runs(text)` encodes `text` this way at the level of Unicode scalar values: it returns a vector of `(scalar, run length)` pairs, one per maximal run of **adjacent** equal scalars, in text order.

A Rust `String` is UTF-8, so one scalar can take 1 to 4 bytes, and what a reader sees as one character can be several scalars (Book ch. 8.2, "Bytes and Scalar Values and Grapheme Clusters! Oh My!"). This task works on scalars, which `text.chars()` yields one at a time (Book ch. 8.2, "Methods for Iterating Over Strings"):

- Run lengths count scalars, not bytes: `😀😀` is one run of length 2, although it is 8 bytes.
- A combining mark such as U+0301 is a scalar of its own: `e` + U+0301 gives two runs, and `é` (U+00E9) is a different scalar from `e`.
- Only neighbours merge. `aabaa` gives three runs, `a` twice; counting all occurrences per scalar (with a map) is a different task.
- Whitespace, NUL and every other scalar are encoded like letters. Empty text gives an empty vector.

Build the result with `push` and grow the last run in place: read the last element with indexing (`out[len - 1]`, Book ch. 8.1, "Reading Elements of Vectors") and add 1 to its count when the next scalar matches it.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::runs("book")
Expected:   vec![('b',1),('o',2),('k',1)]
The two `o`s form one run.

Expression: crate::runs("ééa")
Expected:   vec![('é',2),('a',1)]
Lengths count scalars.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `text` is valid UTF-8 of at most 100,000 bytes.
- No closures or iterator methods; use a `for` loop over `text.chars()`.
hints: Only the most recent run can ever grow. Each new scalar either extends it or starts a new run.
For each `c` in `text.chars()`: let `len = out.len()`. If `len > 0` and `out[len - 1].0 == c`, add 1 to `out[len - 1].1`; otherwise `push((c, 1))`.
`let mut out: Vec<(char, usize)> = Vec::new(); for c in text.chars() { let len = out.len(); if len > 0 && out[len - 1].0 == c { out[len - 1].1 += 1; } else { out.push((c, 1)); } } out`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Scan the scalars once. Compare each scalar with the scalar of the last pair in the output: if they match, increment that pair's count through indexing; otherwise push a new pair with count 1. The `len > 0` test protects the index on the first scalar.
problems.idiomatic_md: `out[len - 1].1 += 1` updates the tuple inside the vector in place, so no pair is popped and pushed back. A `char` comparison is a comparison of scalar values, which is exactly the unit this encoding uses; working on `bytes()` would split multi-byte scalars into separate runs.

Row 6 catches counting all occurrences of each scalar instead of adjacent runs. Row 17 catches finding each run by restarting from the beginning of the text (for example with `chars().nth`): that version did not finish row 17 within 60 s in a debug build.

problems.title: Pig Latin words
problems.description_md:
This is the second exercise at the end of Book ch. 8: convert text to Pig Latin. `pig_latin(text)` converts every word and returns the converted words joined by single ASCII spaces.

Words are what `text.split_whitespace()` yields (Unicode whitespace, including U+3000, separates them; leading, trailing and repeated whitespace disappears). For each word, look at its first Unicode scalar value:

- If it is one of the ASCII vowels `a e i o u A E I O U`, the result is the whole word followed by `-hay` (`apple` → `apple-hay`).
- Otherwise the first scalar moves to the end: the result is the rest of the word, then `-`, then that scalar, then `ay` (`first` → `irst-fay`). The rest may be empty (`x` → `-xay`).

Only those ten ASCII letters are vowels: `y`, `é`, digits, punctuation, emoji and combining marks are all treated as consonants, and punctuation stays part of its word. No case is changed.

The first scalar can be up to 4 bytes long, so "the rest of the word" must be sliced at a scalar boundary (Book ch. 8.2, "Slicing Strings"). `word.char_indices()` gives the first scalar and the byte offset of the second one; a word of one scalar has an empty rest. Build the output with `push_str` and `push` (Book ch. 8.2, "Updating a String"), adding a space before every word except the first.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::pig_latin("first apple")
Expected:   "irst-fay apple-hay".to_string()
Both rules, one word each.

Expression: crate::pig_latin("école 東京")
Expected:   "cole-éay 京-東ay".to_string()
`é` and `東` are consonants here.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `text` is valid UTF-8 of at most 100,000 bytes.
- No closures or iterator methods; walk the words with `for` loops.
hints: For each word you need two things: its first scalar, and the byte offset where the rest begins. Everything else is string building.

In `for (i, c) in word.char_indices()`, the first item gives `first = c`; the second item's `i` is where the rest starts, so `break` there. Start that offset at `word.len()` so a one-scalar word has an empty rest. `"aeiouAEIOU".contains(first)` tests for a vowel.

Before each word, `if !out.is_empty() { out.push(' '); }`. Vowel: `out.push_str(word); out.push_str("-hay");`. Otherwise: `out.push_str(&word[rest..]); out.push('-'); out.push(first); out.push_str("ay");`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Walk the words. For each one, read the first scalar and the byte offset of the next scalar from `char_indices`. Append a separating space unless the output is still empty, then append either the word with `-hay`, or the slice after the first scalar followed by `-`, the first scalar and `ay`. Because every word is non-empty, the output is empty only before the first word.
problems.idiomatic_md: Slicing `&word[rest..]` at an offset from `char_indices` is always on a scalar boundary, so it never panics, even when the first scalar is a 4-byte emoji. Appending into one `String` with `push_str` avoids building a temporary `String` per word; `str::contains` with a `char` checks the vowel set in one call.

Call `crate::pig_latin(t)` and compare with the oracle: split `t` at runs of space, tab, LF and U+3000; convert each word by the two rules above (vowels are exactly `aeiouAEIOU`); join the results with one ASCII space. Use the common generator, seed `0x08000020`, exactly 300 cases.

problems.title: Deterministic token index
problems.description_md:
A book index lists each word with the lines it appears on. `index(text)` builds one for `text`: a vector of `(word, line numbers)` pairs, sorted by word, where each list holds the distinct line numbers on which the word occurs, in ascending order.

- Lines are what `text.lines()` yields (Book ch. 8.2, "Methods for Iterating Over Strings"): the text is split at `\n`, a `\r` just before a `\n` is removed, and a final line ending does not start an extra line. Lines are numbered from 1, and empty or blank lines still count.
- Words are what `line.split_whitespace()` yields; they compare exactly (case, punctuation and Unicode form matter). U+3000 separates words but does not end a line.
- A word that occurs several times on one line lists that line **once**.

Because lines are processed in order, each word's list comes out ascending without sorting it.

The map's iteration order is arbitrary, so gather the pairs into a `Vec` and `sort` it by word (Rust's byte-wise `str` order). The result owns its words and does not borrow `text`.

problems.title: Collection transaction tape
problems.description_md:
A stock ledger replays a tape of operations against a `HashMap<String, u32>` from item name to quantity, starting empty. `transactions(ops)` takes ownership of the tape and returns two things: one `bool` per operation, in tape order, saying whether it succeeded; and the final stock as `(name, quantity)` pairs sorted by name.

The tape is a vector of enums (Book ch. 8.1, "Using an Enum to Store Multiple Types"):

- `Add(name, q)` always succeeds. A missing name starts at 0 (`entry(name).or_insert(0)`, Book ch. 8.3, "Adding a Key and Value Only If a Key Isn't Present"); then `q` is added with `saturating_add`, so the quantity stops at `u32::MAX` instead of overflowing (Chapter 3, "Integer Overflow"). `Add(name, 0)` creates an entry with quantity 0.
- `Take(name, q)` succeeds only if `name` is present and its quantity is at least `q`; then `q` is subtracted. Otherwise it fails and changes nothing. A missing name fails even for `q == 0`. An entry that reaches 0 stays in the map.
- `Remove(name)` succeeds if `name` is present and deletes the entry; on a missing name it fails (`remove` returns `None`, Book ch. 8.3).

Look up the quantity for `Take` with `get_mut`, which gives `Option<&mut u32>` (L8.6). Names compare exactly (case, spaces and Unicode form matter; the empty name is valid). The map's iteration order is arbitrary, so gather the final pairs into a `Vec` and `sort` it.

```text
Expression: crate::transactions(vec![crate::Operation::Add("rust".to_string(),5),crate::Operation::Take("rust".to_string(),7),crate::Operation::Take("rust".to_string(),2)])
Expected:   (vec![true,false,true],vec![("rust".to_string(),3)])
Taking 7 of 5 fails; taking 2 leaves 3.

Expression: crate::transactions(vec![])
Expected:   (vec![],vec![])
Nothing happens.
```

- `ops` has 0 to 100,000 operations; quantities are any `u32`; the names together are at most 1,000,000 bytes of valid UTF-8.
- Keep the `Operation` enum and its derives exactly as given; the tests build operations with `crate::Operation::…`.
hints: Each operation produces one flag and changes the map at most once. Decide success before changing anything, so a failed `Take` leaves the stock alone.
`Operation::Add(name, q)`: `let stock = map.entry(name).or_insert(0); *stock = stock.saturating_add(q); true`. `Operation::Remove(name)`: `map.remove(&name).is_some()`.

`Operation::Take(name, q)`: `match map.get_mut(&name) { Some(stock) => if *stock >= q { *stock -= q; true } else { false }, None => false }`. Push each flag; at the end move the map into a `Vec`, `sort` it, and return `(flags, stock)`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Consume the tape in order and `match` each operation to a `bool`. `Add` goes through `entry` and saturates; `Take` checks presence and sufficiency through `get_mut` before subtracting; `Remove` reports whether `remove` found the key. Push every flag. Finally move the map's pairs into a vector and sort it by name.
problems.idiomatic_md: Matching on the owned `Operation` moves each name straight into the map for `Add`, and `get_mut` updates the quantity in place without a second lookup. `saturating_add` states the overflow policy in the code instead of relying on a debug-build panic.

problems.title: Text catalogue merge
problems.description_md:
`catalogue(text)` reads a list of `category:item` records, one per line, and returns every category with its distinct items: a vector of `(category, items)` pairs sorted by category, each `items` list sorted too.

Parse each line from `text.lines()` (Book ch. 8.2, "Methods for Iterating Over Strings") like this:

1. Find the **first** ASCII colon `:`. A line without one is ignored. Later colons belong to the item (`time:10:30` has item `10:30`). Look for it with `char_indices`, which gives byte offsets that are safe to slice at (Book ch. 8.2, "Slicing Strings"); the colon is one byte, so the item starts at the next offset.
2. The category is the text before the colon and the item the text after it, each with leading and trailing Unicode whitespace removed by `trim` (so U+3000 and tabs are removed too, but inner spaces stay).
3. If either side is empty after trimming, the line is ignored.

Collect the items in a `HashMap<String, HashSet<String>>`: `entry(category).or_default()` gives the category's set (Book ch. 8.3, "Updating a Hash Map"), and inserting into a `HashSet` (L8.6) drops repeated items. Neither the map nor the sets have a usable order, so move each set into a `Vec` and `sort` it, then sort the outer list. Sorting uses Rust's byte-wise `str` order: uppercase before lowercase, `é` after ASCII. Nothing else is normalized: case, inner whitespace and Unicode form all matter, and a full-width colon `：` (U+FF1A) is not a separator.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::catalogue("fruit:apple\nveg:kale\nfruit:fig")
Expected:   vec![("fruit".to_string(),vec!["apple".to_string(),"fig".to_string()]),("veg".to_string(),vec!["kale".to_string()])]
`fruit` collects two items.

Expression: crate::catalogue("")
Expected:   vec![]
No lines at all.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `text` is valid UTF-8 of at most 100,000 bytes.
- No closures or iterator methods (`find` with a closure, `split_once` and the like are not needed); use `for` loops.
hints: Split the work into: find the first colon in a line; trim and validate the two sides; add the item to its category's set; and at the end turn the nested map into sorted vectors.

`let mut colon = None; for (i, c) in line.char_indices() { if c == ':' { colon = Some(i); break; } }`. Then `if let Some(i) = colon { let key = line[..i].trim(); let item = line[i + 1..].trim(); … }`.

Store with `groups.entry(key.to_string()).or_default().insert(item.to_string());` when both are non-empty. Then `for (key, items) in groups { let mut list = Vec::new(); for item in items { list.push(item); } list.sort(); out.push((key, list)); } out.sort();`.
problems.solution_approach_md: For each line, locate the first `:` by walking `char_indices` and stop there. Slice and trim both sides; skip the line if there is no colon or a side is empty. Insert the owned item into the set that `entry(...).or_default()` returns for the owned category. Finally, for each category, move its set's items into a vector and sort it, push the pair, and sort the list of pairs by category.
problems.idiomatic_md: A `HashMap` whose values are `HashSet`s groups and deduplicates in one structure, and `or_default()` creates each inner set on first use. Slicing at `i + 1` is safe because `:` is a one-byte scalar, so the next scalar starts right after it. Sorting both levels at the end is what makes the output independent of hash order.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `count = pick(30)`, then `count` lines. For each line draw the category with `pick(5)` from `["A", "é", "東", "", " A "]`, the item with `pick(5)` from `["x", "😀", "e\u{301}", "", " y:z "]`, and `valid = (pick(3) != 0)`; the line is category + (`:` if `valid`, else `;`) + item. Join the lines with LF (no final LF). Call `crate::catalogue(text)` and compare with the oracle: the parsing rules above applied by a separate implementation (first `:`, trim space, tab, LF, CR and U+3000 at both ends, skip empty sides), each category's distinct items sorted, categories sorted, both by UTF-8 bytes. Note that an invalid line such as `A; y:z ` still contains a colon, inside the item, and is parsed at that colon. Use the common generator, seed `0x08000023`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases with a category of 2 or more values 220; cases where " A " and "A" merge after trimming 186; cases with an empty catalogue 24. Over all generated lines: lines accepted at the drawn separator 1719; lines without a colon 1134; lines ignored for an empty side 997; lines accepted at a colon inside the drawn value 275.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

Row 5 catches splitting at the last colon, row 4 catches not trimming, and row 12 catches trimming ASCII whitespace only. Rows 10 and 11 fail for output in set or map order. Row 18 checks scale; a `Vec` with `contains` for each category's items instead of a `HashSet` still finishes it in about 0.1 s, so the set is required by the description rather than by timing.

problems.title: Employee directory
problems.description_md:
This is the Book's Chapter 8 exercise: keep a company directory that assigns employees to departments, lists the people in one department, and lists everyone by department, all in alphabetical order, behind a small text interface. You edit one file, `src/lib.rs`. Runtime rows include that file as a module, glob-import it at the harness crate root and call it as `crate::Directory`.

**Part 1**

The starter gives `Directory` two private maps. `departments` maps a department name to the names of the employees in it; `homes` maps an employee's name to their department. Every method must leave the two maps agreeing: a name is a key of `homes` exactly when it appears once, in the list of the department `homes` gives for it. `Directory::new()` returns an empty directory.

Write `add(&mut self, name: &str, department: &str) -> bool`. Trim surrounding whitespace (as `trim` does, including U+3000) from both arguments; inside text, spaces, case and every other character are kept. Names and departments are compared exactly: case-sensitively and without Unicode normalization.

- If either trimmed argument is empty, return `false` and change nothing.
- If the employee is already in that department, return `false` and change nothing.
- If the employee is in a different department, move them: take the name out of the old department's list, remove that department's entry if nobody is left in it, then add them to the new department and return `true`.
- Otherwise add the employee to the department, creating its entry if needed, and return `true`.

**Part 2**

`department(&self, name: &str) -> Vec<String>` trims the query and returns the names in that department, sorted ascending in `String` order (by UTF-8 bytes, so upper case comes before lower case and `"10"` before `"9"`). A department nobody is in gives an empty vector.

`all(&self) -> Vec<(String, Vec<String>)>` returns every department that has at least one employee, sorted by department name in `String` order, each paired with its sorted names. Do not rely on the map's iteration order: copy the keys into a `Vec` and sort it. Both methods return owned copies, so changing a returned vector never changes the directory.

**Part 3**

`remove(&mut self, name: &str) -> bool` trims the name. If that exact employee is in the directory, take them out of `homes` and out of their department's list (removing the department's entry if it becomes empty) and return `true`. Otherwise return `false` and change nothing.

**Part 4**

`command(&mut self, line: &str) -> String` is the text interface. It splits `line` into words with `split_whitespace` and returns the reply; every reply line ends with `\n`. The first word is the command, matched case-sensitively; names and departments in a command are the remaining words joined with single spaces.

- `Add <name> to <department>`: the name is the words between `Add` and the first word that is exactly `to`; the department is every word after that `to`. If there is no `to`, or no word before it, or no word after it, reply `Usage: Add <name> to <department>` and change nothing. Otherwise reply `Added <name> to <department>` for a new employee, `Moved <name> to <department>` for an employee who was in another department, or `<name> is already in <department>`, and apply `add`.
- `List <department>`: reply `<department>: ` followed by that department's sorted names joined with `, `, or `<department>: (none)` when nobody is in it. With no department words, reply `Usage: List <department>`.
- `Remove <name>`: reply `Removed <name>` when `remove` succeeds, otherwise `<name> is not in the directory`. With no name words, reply `Usage: Remove <name>`.
- `All`: one `<department>: <names>` line per department, in the order `all` gives; `(no employees)` when the directory is empty. Any word after `All` makes the reply `Usage: All`.
- An empty line, or any other first word (including `add` or `ADD`), gives `Unknown command`.
problems.constraints_md:
- At most 100,000 employees in a directory at once; each name, department and command line is valid UTF-8 of at most 100,000 bytes. NUL, newlines and any other scalar values are ordinary text; whitespace is what `char::is_whitespace` accepts, as used by `trim` and `split_whitespace`.
- No case folding and no Unicode normalization: `ada`/`Ada` and `é`/`e` + U+0301 are different names.
- Keep the two private map fields of the starter; no `BTreeMap`, `BTreeSet` or `VecDeque`.
- Chapters 1–8 only: no closures or closure-taking methods, no `?`, no traits, generics or lifetimes of your own.
hints: The two maps answer different questions: `homes` says in one lookup which department a person is in now, and `departments` says who is in a department. Each change has to update both, or a later `add` or `remove` will act on stale information.

In `add`, trim and validate first, then look the name up in `homes`. To move someone, find the name's position in the old department's `Vec` with a loop, `remove` it, and drop the department with `self.departments.remove(…)` once its list is empty; then `entry(department.to_string()).or_default().push(…)` and `homes.insert(…)`. For sorted output, copy the keys into a `Vec<String>`, `sort` it, and look each one up.

In `command`, `let mut words = Vec::new(); for w in line.split_whitespace() { words.push(w); }` gives a `Vec<&str>`; `match words[0] { "Add" => …, "List" => …, … }` picks the command (check `words.is_empty()` first). Find the first `to` with `for (i, word) in rest.iter().enumerate()`, and rebuild a name from `&rest[..i]` with a small helper that pushes the words separated by one space.
problems.solution_approach_md: `add` trims both arguments and rejects an empty one. It looks the name up in `homes`: the same department means `false`; a different one means the name is taken out of the old list by a `while` loop and `Vec::remove`, and the old department's entry is removed when its list becomes empty, so `all` never sees an empty department. The name is then pushed through `entry(…).or_default()` and recorded in `homes`. `department` clones the list (or starts from an empty one) and sorts it; `all` collects and sorts the keys, then builds each pair with `department`. `remove` takes the name out of `homes` first (`HashMap::remove` returns the department) and then out of the list. `command` splits the line into a `Vec<&str>`, dispatches on the first word, rebuilds names and departments with a word-joining helper, decides between `Added`, `Moved` and `already in` by looking in `homes` before calling `add`, and formats each department line with one helper shared by `List` and `All`.
problems.idiomatic_md: A second map used as an index (`homes`) turns "is this person already somewhere?" from a scan of every department into one lookup, at the cost of an invariant every method must keep; sorting only at the output boundary is what makes code built on `HashMap` give the same answer on every run.
problems.random_md:
Reset the 32-bit LCG to seed `0x08010000` once. next() updates state = (1664525 × state + 1013904223) mod 2^32 and returns it; pick(k) = (next() >> 16) % k. Generate 300 cases. Each case starts from `crate::Directory::new()` and performs 20 operations; each operation first draws op=pick(4). op 0 calls `add(N[pick(8)], D[pick(6)])` (the name is drawn first). op 1 calls `remove(N[pick(8)])`. op 2 calls `department(D[pick(6)])`. op 3 calls `command(line)`, where form=pick(6) chooses the line: form 0 is `"Add " + W[pick(5)] + " to " + E[pick(4)]` (W drawn first), form 1 is `"List " + E[pick(4)]`, form 2 is `"Remove " + W[pick(5)]`, form 3 is `"All"`, form 4 is `"Add " + W[pick(5)]`, and form 5 is J[pick(3)]. The lists are N = `["Ada", " Ada ", "ada", "é", "e\u{301}", "東京", "\u{3000}😀", ""]`, D = `["Ops", " Ops\t", "ops", "営業", "\u{3000}", ""]`, W = `["Ada", "é", "東京", "e\u{301}", "Sally Ann"]`, E = `["Ops", "Back to School", "営業", "ops"]` and J = `["", "add Ada to Ops", "All all"]`; their empty, whitespace-only, differently cased and differently composed entries weight the draws toward the rejection and exact-match boundaries.

The independent oracle keeps a single name-to-department dictionary and no department lists: it trims, rejects an empty side, and moves or refuses by comparing the stored department; department lists and `all()` are derived by filtering the dictionary and sorting by UTF-8 bytes; command replies are built from the Part 4 rules. After every operation, compare the operation's result and the complete `all()` with the oracle.

Realized coverage over the 6,000 operations: `add` 702 new employees, 112 moves, 57 already in the department, 626 rejected for an empty side; `remove` 263 true, 1,250 false; `department` 305 non-empty and 1,184 empty answers; `command` replies `Added` 208, `Moved` 33, `already in` 16, Add usage 227, `List` with names 58, `List` `(none)` 191, `Removed` 53, `not in the directory` 214, `All` with lines 174, `(no employees)` 80, `Usage: All` 73, `Unknown command` 174. The forms never produce `List` or `Remove` without words; rows 34 and 35 cover those usage replies. The reference solution and the oracle agree on all 6,000 results and snapshots.

- Required: `Directory` has exactly the two private fields `departments: HashMap<String, Vec<String>>` and `homes: HashMap<String, String>` from the starter; no `BTreeMap`, `BTreeSet` or `VecDeque` appears in the file.

problems.title: The catalogue
problems.description_md:
The library gets a catalogue: one `Library` value that owns every book in a `Vec<Book>` and every member in a `HashMap<u32, Member>`, hands out book ids, answers queries, and runs checkouts and returns through the LM6 methods.

**Part 1**

The starter is the Accepted LM7 package, unchanged, plus a new file `src/library.rs` that holds the `Library` struct with its three private fields (`books: Vec<Book>`, `members: HashMap<u32, Member>`, `next_book_id: u32`), a finished `new` and every other method signature with a placeholder body. The file is not part of the crate yet: declare `pub mod library;` in `src/lib.rs` and re-export `pub use library::Library;` beside the existing re-exports, so callers can write `library::Library` (and `crate::Library` inside the package).

`Library::new()` has no books, no members and `next_book_id` 1. `add_book(title, author, year)` stores `Book::new(id, title, author, year)` (so the title is normalized and the author trimmed as in LM4) under the next id and returns that id: ids start at 1, go up by 1 with every call, and are never reused, even for equal titles. `add_member(id, name, premium)` inserts `Member::new(id, name, premium)` and returns `true` only if no member has that id; otherwise it returns `false` and keeps the existing member unchanged. `book(id)` and `member(id)` return a shared reference to the stored record, or `None` (id 0, for example, is never a book).

**Part 2**

`books_by(author)` returns references to the books whose author equals the query after both are trimmed and lower-cased with `to_lowercase` (no other case folding, no Unicode normalization), ordered by `sort_key(&book.title)` in case-sensitive `&str` order and then by id. `search_titles(query)` returns, in ascending order, the ids of the books for which `title_matches(&book.title, query)` is true; the empty query matches every book. `authors()` returns each distinct stored author once, compared exactly, sorted in `String` order. `count_by_status()` returns `(available, borrowed, lost)`. LM8's public API cannot make a book `Lost` (`mark_lost` needs a `&mut Book`, and `Library` lends only `&Book`), so the third count is 0 in every test; it is still counted so a later milestone can use it.

**Part 3**

`checkout(book_id, member_id, today)` returns `false` and changes nothing when either id is unknown; otherwise it returns `Book::checkout` called on the stored book with the stored member, which keeps every LM6 rule (only an available book, limits 3 and 6, due day `today + 14` or `today + 28`, atomic rejection). `return_book(book_id, today)` returns `None` when the book is unknown or not borrowed; otherwise it reads the borrower's id from the book's status, finds that stored member, and returns `Book::return_to_shelf`: the LM3 late fee in cents, with the book available again and the member's count reduced. Checkout days are at most `u32::MAX - 28`; return days may be any `u32`.

**Part 4**

Everything else stays as LM7 left it. `fees.rs`, `text.rs`, `book.rs`, `member.rs` and the menu in `src/main.rs` are unchanged, and the menu is not connected to the catalogue yet. The LM6 regression suite and the exact menu transcripts still pass.
problems.constraints_md: All LM1–LM7 contracts remain unchanged. At most 100,000 `add_book` calls per `Library`, so the `u32` id counter cannot overflow; at most 100,000 members; every text argument is valid UTF-8 of at most 100,000 bytes. Member ids use the full `u32` range and years the full `u16` range. Checkout days are at most `u32::MAX - 28`; return days accept every `u32`. Chapters 1–8 only: no closures or closure-taking methods, no `?` or `Result`, no traits, generics or lifetime annotations of your own. The package is named `library` (edition 2024, no dependencies) and contains exactly `src/lib.rs`, `src/fees.rs`, `src/text.rs`, `src/book.rs`, `src/member.rs`, `src/library.rs` and `src/main.rs`.
hints: `book` and `member` lend the stored records, so they need no clone: `self.members.get(&id)` is already an `Option<&Member>`, and a `for book in &self.books` loop can return `Some(book)`.

To order `books_by` without a closure, collect tuples `(sort_key(&book.title), book.id, index)` and call `sort()`: tuples compare field by field, so this sorts by key and then by id; then push `&self.books[index]` for each tuple. For `authors`, `HashSet::insert` returns `false` for a value the set already holds, which tells you whether an author is new.

In `checkout`, find the book's index with a loop first (that shared borrow then ends), then `let Some(member) = self.members.get_mut(&member_id) else { return false; };` and finish with `self.books[i].checkout(member, today)`: `books` and `members` are different fields, so both borrows can be live at once. In `return_book`, `self.books[i].borrower()` gives the member id to look up.
problems.solution_approach_md: `src/lib.rs` gains `pub mod library;` and `pub use library::Library;`. In `library.rs`, a private `index_of` loop maps a book id to its position in `books`. `add_book` reads and increments `next_book_id` and pushes `Book::new`; `add_member` checks `contains_key` before `insert`. `book` scans the vector and `member` is a map `get`. `books_by` lower-cases the trimmed query once, gathers `(sort_key, id, index)` tuples for the matching books, sorts them and maps the indexes back to references. `search_titles` keeps the ids of matching titles; the vector is already in ascending id order because books are only ever pushed with increasing ids. `authors` pushes each author the first time a `HashSet<&str>` accepts it and sorts the result. `count_by_status` matches every status. `checkout` and `return_book` use `let ... else` to stop at an unknown id, then hand the stored book and member to the LM6 methods, so no transaction rule is written twice.
problems.idiomatic_md: A collection type that owns its records and lends them out by reference keeps one copy of every book and member; delegating each transaction to the methods that already enforce its rules means the catalogue adds lookup, not new places for those rules to drift apart.
problems.random_md:
Row 38. Reset the 32-bit LCG to seed `0x08020000` once; next() updates state = (1664525 × state + 1013904223) mod 2^32 and returns it, and pick(k) = (next() >> 16) % k. Generate 300 cases. Each case starts from `Library::new()` and adds `3 + pick(5)` books with `add_book(T[pick(6)], A[pick(5)], 0)` (title drawn first). It then makes three `add_member` calls with name `"M"`: the first with id 0, the other two with id P[pick(4)]; each call then draws premium = (pick(2) == 1). Then it performs 20 operations; each draws op=pick(6), and n is the number of books at that moment. op 0 is `add_book(T[pick(6)], A[pick(5)], 0)`. ops 1, 2 and 3 are `checkout`: the book id is `1 + pick(n)` when pick(4) != 0, otherwise `[0, n + 1][pick(2)]` (both absent); then the member id is MQ[pick(6)] and the day OUT[pick(4)]. op 4 is `return_book`: draw pick(3); if it is not 0 and some book is borrowed, the book id is the smallest borrowed id, otherwise it is pick(n + 2); then the day is RET[pick(14)]. op 5 queries `books_by(A[pick(5)])` (as ids), `search_titles(QS[pick(4)])` and `authors()`. The lists are T = `["The Cat", "cat", "A Dog", "Dog", "an Owl", "東京"]`, A = `["Ann", " ann ", "ANN", "Bob", "Émile"]`, QS = `["", "CAT", "dog", "x"]`, P = `[0, 1, 2, 4294967295]`, MQ = `[0, 0, 0, 1, 4294967295, 3]` (3 is never a member), OUT = `[0, 7, 100, 4294967267]` and RET = `[0, 14, 15, 21, 22, 28, 29, 35, 36, 57, 58, 71, 72, 4294967295]`.

After the member setup and after every operation, compare the result, `count_by_status()`, `book(id)` for every id from 0 to n + 1 and `member(id)` for the ids 0, 1, 2, 4294967295 and 3 with the independent oracle. The oracle keeps plain dictionaries of books (normalized title, trimmed author, status) and members (premium, count) and applies the LM3–LM6 rules directly: limit 3 or 6, due day +14 or +28, fee min(2000, 25·min(late, 7) + 50·max(late − 7, 0)) with late = max(day − due, 0), count floored at zero, and every rejection leaving both records unchanged; the queries are computed by filtering and sorting. Realized coverage: `add_member` 678 new and 222 duplicate ids; `checkout` 567 standard and 581 premium successes (279 of them on day 4294967267), 765 unknown books, 737 unknown members, 315 books not available, 28 standard members at their limit (the premium limit is not reached; row 26 covers it); `return_book` 322 on time, 29 in the 25-cent tier, 89 in the 50-cent tier, 46 capped, 152 unknown books, 350 books not borrowed; `books_by` 882 non-empty answers (698 with two or more books, where the order matters) and 105 empty ones. The reference solution and the oracle agree on all 6,300 snapshots.

Row 37. Reset the 32-bit LCG to seed `0x06020000` once; next() uses the recurrence above. Generate cases i=0..299. Each case consumes exactly three draws: member_id=next(), due=next(), raw_day=next(). Let mode=i%10 and premium=(i//10)%2==1. Let limit be 6 for premium, otherwise 3. Book metadata is (id=1,title="x",author="y",year=1); member name is "A". Modes 0–3 start Available and call checkout at today=raw_day%4294967268; initial borrowed is respectively 0, limit, 255, limit-1. Modes 4 and 5 start Lost or Borrowed{member_id,due_day:due}, borrowed=0, then attempt checkout at that same permitted today. Modes 6–9 call return_to_shelf: mode 6 starts Borrowed with matching ID and count 1; mode 7 starts Borrowed with borrower ID member_id XOR 1 and count 1; mode 8 starts Available with count 0; mode 9 starts Borrowed with matching ID and count alternating 0/255 according to (i//10)%2. For return modes override due_day to 100 (the draw is still consumed); choose today from [99,100,101,107,108,143,144,4294967295][(i//10)%8]. The independent oracle uses state and limit comparisons; successful checkout increments once and sets due today+14/28. Rejected operations preserve both complete records. Matching returns produce Some(min(2000,25*min(late,7)+50*max(late-7,0))) with late=max(today-100,0), set Available, and floor the decremented count at zero. Compare the result and complete Book and Member records after every call.

This is the LM6 regression suite, unchanged and carried forward from LM7 through the crate-root re-exports `Book`, `Status` and `Member`. It is regression coverage, not a new Chapter 8 feature. Realized: 60 successful and 120 rejected checkouts, 60 fee-paying and 60 rejected returns; the LM8 reference and the oracle agree on all 300 cases.
